Extend the test for another two weeks — a 7-day price window is too short to know whether the wrong-call rate is a real, lasting shift.
explanation: Option B is correct: Hopper's entire product promise is that its recommendation is worth trusting over just booking whenever, and a near-doubling of the rate at which its top recommendation, 'Book Now', turns out to be wrong is a direct hit to that promise, not a side cost to weigh against a conversion number. The conversion lift is coming substantially from the same mechanism that's producing more wrong calls: recommending 'Book Now' more often mechanically increases both bookings and the odds any given one was premature. A tool users increasingly can't trust to call this right is a worse product even with more bookings in the short window. Option A treats the conversion lift as sufficient on its own and waves off the guardrail with 'never perfect,' but there's a difference between an already-accepted baseline error rate and one that's nearly doubled during the exact test being evaluated — that shift is the guardrail doing its job, not something to explain away. Option C's isolation idea is reasonable in spirit but describes work that would require a new test, not a decision on the test already run; 'ship part of it' isn't an available option against data that only exists for the bundled change. Option D's timing objection doesn't hold up — the wrong-call rate is already measured on the same 7-day window Hopper uses to grade every recommendation, both before and during the test, so the comparison is apples-to-apples and doesn't need a longer look to be trusted.
hints: Ask what Hopper is actually selling its users, and what happens to that promise if the tool's top call is wrong much more often.
The conversion lift and the rising wrong-call rate may not be two separate costs to weigh — check whether they're coming from the same underlying mechanism.

title: Poshmark's listing-share drop — the analyst's two-hour verdict
scenario_context: Poshmark's daily listing-share count, users resharing another seller's listing to their own followers, fell 22% over one week. An analyst investigates for two hours and reports: 'Instagram just changed its API rate limits, which broke our one-tap cross-post-to-Instagram button — that's obviously why shares are down, since cross-posting is the most popular way people share.' The share-drop ticket is closed with this explanation.
description: What's the flaw in the analyst's conclusion?
options: The analyst never checked whether the drop is concentrated among users who cross-post, versus everyone else on the platform.
There's no flaw — a broken cross-post button is a well-known cause of share drops, and the timing makes the explanation obviously correct.
The flaw is the metric itself; Poshmark should track closet views instead of shares, since shares are a noisier signal of real interest.
Two hours isn't enough investigation time; the analyst should have spent at least a full day before reaching any conclusion.
explanation: Option A is correct: the analyst has one plausible-sounding hypothesis, a broken integration, and never ran the one check that would confirm or kill it — splitting the 22% drop by whether the affected users actually rely on cross-posting to Instagram at all. If the API break is really the cause, the drop should concentrate almost entirely among users who habitually cross-post, and in-app-only sharers should show no change; if the drop is roughly uniform across both groups, something else, unrelated to the Instagram integration, is happening platform-wide. A timing coincidence and a plausible mechanism aren't the same as a validated diagnosis. Option B accepts the story on plausibility and timing alone, exactly the shortcut a structured investigation exists to catch — a well-known failure mode being possible doesn't mean it's confirmed here. Option C sidesteps the actual question, whether the stated cause explains the observed drop, by proposing a different metric to track instead; changing what's measured next quarter doesn't validate or invalidate this week's explanation. Option D's fix is just 'spend more time,' but the issue isn't investigation duration, it's that the one hypothesis formed was never actually tested against a segment cut — a longer clock without that check wouldn't have caught the gap either.
hints: The analyst found one plausible story and stopped. What single split of the data would actually confirm whether that specific story is true?
If a broken integration is really the cause, only a specific group of users should be affected. Has anyone checked who that group is versus who else dropped?

title: Gusto's Auto-File feature — a rare tax error with a real penalty behind it
scenario_context: Gusto ships an 'Auto-File' feature that automatically files state payroll taxes on a small business's behalf, removing a manual step. Adoption is strong: 68% of eligible accounts turn it on within a month, and support-ticket volume for tax filing drops sharply. A quality audit finds Auto-File incorrectly applies a rarely-used multi-state tax rule for about 0.3% of filings, a rate the compliance team calls low but that has already caused two customers to receive state penalty notices.
description: What's the most defensible strategic call?
options: Keep Auto-File live as-is — a 0.3% error rate is low by any reasonable statistical standard, and two isolated penalty notices don't establish a pattern.
Disable Auto-File entirely until the multi-state rule is fixed, even though the vast majority of filings are unaffected and reverting removes a strongly-adopted feature.
Keep Auto-File live for single-state filers, where the error doesn't apply, and pause it specifically for the multi-state filing population until the rule is fixed.
Keep Auto-File live, but add a disclaimer at filing time stating Gusto isn't liable for state tax errors, shifting the exposure back to the customer.
explanation: Option C is correct: the failure is precisely scoped, a specific multi-state rule, not a general reliability problem, so the defensible move is a scoped one — keep the feature live where it works correctly and pause exactly the population where it doesn't, rather than an all-or-nothing call. This protects the adoption and support-load wins for the large majority of unaffected customers while stopping new penalty exposure for the specific segment at risk, and it's the option that actually matches the shape of what the audit found. Option A treats a low error rate as automatically acceptable, but the discriminating fact here isn't the rate, it's what the error causes: a payroll product's core promise is compliance, and this feature is actively generating real state penalty notices for customers who trusted it to handle exactly this. A statistically small rate of a trust-breaking outcome isn't the same as a statistically small rate of a minor inconvenience. Option B swings to the opposite extreme, reverting a strongly-adopted feature entirely, discarding a real win for the large majority of customers where the rule in question never even applies — a broader response than the scoped failure calls for. Option D tries to solve the problem with a disclaimer rather than a fix, but shifting liability language doesn't stop Gusto's system from filing incorrectly; small businesses are exactly the customer base least equipped to catch a payroll tax error themselves, and a disclaimer doesn't restore the trust the feature is meant to provide.
hints: The audit found a failure scoped to one specific condition, not a general reliability problem. Ask whether the response needs to be all-or-nothing or can be scoped the same way.
A payroll product's core promise is different from a typical feature's — weigh what a low-probability error actually causes here, not just how low the probability is.

title: Hinge's match rate drops three points — concentrated in three campaign-heavy markets
scenario_context: Hinge's platform-wide match rate, the share of likes that result in a mutual match, fell from 8.2% to 6.9% over three weeks, with no app release in that window. A regional breakdown shows the drop is concentrated entirely in three large metro markets that recently had a surge of new sign-ups from a single paid-acquisition campaign; every other market's match rate is flat versus three weeks ago.
description: What's the most defensible next step?
options: Report the platform-wide 6.9% as the current match rate and move on, since the number is already correctly computed.
Check whether this campaign's sign-ups differ in profile-completion or usage pattern from typical organic users in those markets.
Pause the paid-acquisition campaign immediately in all three markets, since it's clearly the cause of a declining core metric.
Extend the observation window to six weeks before drawing any conclusion, since three weeks may not be enough time for new users to become active daters.
explanation: Option B is correct: the segmentation has already done real work, isolating the drop to three markets that share one recent change, a surge of sign-ups from a specific paid campaign, while every other market stayed flat. The next step is testing the specific mechanism that would explain it: if this campaign's sign-ups have thinner profiles, different photo quality, or lower early engagement than typical organic users in the same markets, that population entering the like-and-match pool would mechanically drag down the aggregate match rate in exactly those three markets without anything changing about the product or about existing users. Option A stops at the number the segmentation just explained — moving on without checking the mechanism throws away the exact lead the breakdown surfaced; reporting a rate without understanding why it moved is the failure mode a structured diagnosis exists to avoid. Option C reaches for an operational decision, killing the campaign, before confirming the mechanism at all; if it turns out to be a fixable profile-completion nudge rather than an inherent flaw in the acquisition source, pausing the campaign is a bigger and more costly move than the evidence yet supports. Option D's longer window doesn't test the specific, already-narrowed hypothesis in hand, it just delays looking at the one lead the segment cut already handed the team.
hints: The segment cut already pointed at one specific, recent change. What would confirm whether that change is actually the mechanism, not just correlated with it?

A new population entering a rate's denominator can drag the aggregate down even if nothing about the existing product or existing users changed. What would you check about that new population specifically?

title: Oura's morning Readiness push — predicting the opens-versus-depth split
scenario_context: Oura adds a daily morning push notification showing a user's Readiness Score the moment they wake, replacing the previous behavior where users had to open the app to see it. The team's hypothesis is that this makes checking the score more convenient, but doesn't by itself make users engage more deeply with the app's other features (trends, workout recommendations, guided sessions).
description: If this hypothesis is correct, what should happen to (1) daily app opens, and (2) average session length, and why?
options: Daily app opens should rise from the notification itself, while average session length falls as more opens become quick score-checks.
Both daily app opens and average session length should rise together, since any new touchpoint that gets users into the app tends to expose them to more features while they're there.
Daily app opens should stay flat, since a notification only changes how the score is delivered, not whether users were already going to check it.
Average session length should rise while daily app opens stays flat, since the same users are opening the app but now spending more time acting on the score.
explanation: Option A is correct: a notification that surfaces the score directly creates a new, low-effort reason to open the app that didn't require deliberately navigating there before, which should mechanically raise the count of opens. But the hypothesis is explicit that this convenience doesn't by itself deepen engagement with anything else, so the natural signature is more opens that are each shorter on average — quick glance-and-close visits diluting a mix that used to be dominated by more deliberate, feature-browsing sessions. The two metrics should move in opposite directions because they're capturing different things: one counts a new low-effort entry point, the other reflects what happens once someone's actually in the app. Option B predicts both rising together, but that requires the deeper-engagement effect the hypothesis explicitly rules out — a quick notification-driven glance has no particular reason to convert into browsing trends or starting a guided session. Option C misses the direct, mechanical effect of adding a new, lower-effort trigger to open the app at all; a notification that removes a navigation step should increase how often the action happens, that's the most basic consequence of reducing friction to a common check-in. Option D gets the session-length direction backwards, and offers no mechanism for why sessions would lengthen when the changed behavior is specifically a faster, more convenient way to see one number.
hints: Separate what the change makes easier from what it doesn't touch — a faster way to check one number isn't the same as a reason to browse the rest of the app.
One of these two metrics should move for a simple, mechanical reason: a new low-effort trigger increasing how often an action happens. Ask what that does to the mix of session types.

title: Faire's low-MOQ ranking boost — buyer completion up, GMV down
scenario_context: Faire changes its wholesale search ranking to favor brands with lower minimum order quantities (MOQs), reasoning that small independent retailers are more likely to complete an order when the upfront commitment is smaller. Four weeks in: buyer-side order completion rate is up 13%, but average order value is down 21%, and total GMV, orders completed times order value, is down 4% overall. Brand-side, retention of larger, established brands with higher MOQs is down slightly as their search visibility drops.
description: What's the most defensible way to frame this trade-off?
options: This is a clear win — order completion rate is the metric the ranking change targeted, and it improved exactly as intended.
This is a clear loss — GMV, the business's core revenue driver, is down, so the ranking change should revert immediately.
Name the two-sided trade-off — buyer-side completion improved, but GMV fell as higher-value brands lost visibility and retention risk grew.
Reframe entirely around a new metric, number of unique brands purchased from per buyer, since that better reflects marketplace health than either completion or GMV.
explanation: Option C is correct: this result isn't a single number to read in isolation, it's a marketplace-liquidity trade-off with real costs showing up on both sides of the two-sided market. The buyer-side win, easier completion for small retailers, is genuinely real, but it's being funded by de-prioritizing exactly the higher-value, established brands whose order sizes drive GMV, and those same brands are starting to disengage as their visibility drops, which would compound the revenue loss further if it continues. Naming both halves of that trade-off, rather than picking a side, is what a defensible read of a two-sided marketplace result actually requires. Option A isolates the metric the change directly targeted and declares victory, but a ranking change that hits its own target metric while dragging down total GMV and provoking a retention risk among supply-side brands isn't unambiguously working, it's trading one thing for another. Option B swings to the opposite extreme and calls for an immediate revert based on GMV alone, discarding a real and meaningful buyer-side completion gain without weighing whether a smaller, targeted fix, rather than a full reversion, could address the brand-retention risk while keeping the buyer-side win intact. Option D introduces an entirely new metric not evidenced anywhere in the data given, and swapping the yardstick doesn't resolve the actual trade-off already visible in the four weeks of results, it just changes what's being measured instead of confronting what happened.
hints: This is a two-sided marketplace — a change that helps one side's conversion can cost something on the other side. Look for the option that names both halves.
Three numbers moved here, and they didn't all move for the same reason. Check whether one side's gain is structurally connected to the other side's loss before picking a single winner or loser.

title: Credit Karma's approval-likelihood score — does restricting the audience close the gaming hole?
scenario_context: Credit Karma ranks credit card offers partly by a blended 'approval likelihood' score, estimated from how often past users with similar profiles were approved for that card. An analyst notices issuers have begun submitting cards with narrower, hand-picked target segments (e.g., 'excellent credit only, income above $150K') specifically to inflate their approval-likelihood score and climb the ranking, even when the card isn't a strong fit for most Credit Karma users who'd see it. A PM proposes: 'Fix this by only showing a card to users who fall inside the issuer's declared target segment — the score will only ever be computed on people who were likely to be approved anyway.'
description: What's the flaw in the PM's proposed fix?
options: There's no flaw — restricting the audience to the declared segment guarantees the approval-likelihood score reflects only genuinely qualified users, closing the gaming hole.
The issuer still defines their own target segment, so the same narrowing move now also decides who sees the card, leaving the underlying incentive untouched.
The flaw is unrelated to gaming; restricting the audience will simply reduce impressions and hurt Credit Karma's ad revenue from this issuer.
The fix should instead lower the weight of approval-likelihood in the ranking formula entirely, since any weighted score can eventually be gamed.
explanation: Option B is correct: the fix changes who the score gets shown to, but the issuer still controls the very definition being used to narrow that audience — exactly the lever they were already gaming. An issuer that wants to keep climbing the ranking can simply declare an even narrower, more hand-picked segment, both inflating the approval-likelihood score and ensuring the card is now literally only shown to that self-selected slice, which does nothing to fix the ranking for the broader population the recommendation is meant to serve; it just legitimizes the same gaming move as a targeting decision. Option A accepts the PM's framing that restricting the audience solves the problem, but the entire vulnerability was the issuer's control over the segment definition — restricting exposure to that same self-chosen segment doesn't remove issuer control, it formalizes it. Option C raises a real business consideration, but it isn't the question being asked, and it doesn't identify why the fix fails to close the gaming hole itself. Option D proposes a different, more drastic fix without diagnosing what's actually wrong with the proposed one; a lower weight would reduce the impact of the gaming, but the question is specifically whether the audience-restriction fix works, and it doesn't, because the same controllable lever remains in play.
hints: Ask who still controls the exact input the fix relies on to narrow the audience — is it something Credit Karma sets independently, or something the issuer still declares?
A fix that changes who sees a score doesn't close a gaming hole if the same party still controls the definition that determines who that is.

title: Zocdoc's same-day boost — bookings up, no-shows concentrated in the new segment
scenario_context: Zocdoc tests boosting same-day-available appointments higher in search results. Two-week result: completed bookings are up 14%, the stated success metric. The guardrail, the no-show rate for booked appointments, rises from 9% to 15% specifically among same-day bookings, while bookings made more than 2 days in advance show no change in no-show rate.
description: What's the most defensible call?
options: Ship to 100% — a 14% booking lift is substantial, and some rise in no-shows is an expected trade-off of making booking easier.
Hold the rollout — no-shows are climbing specifically among the new same-day bookings, a cost providers bear directly.
Ship only to returning patients who've completed a prior appointment, since new patients are more likely to be the source of the no-show increase.
Extend the test two more weeks to see whether providers adjust their same-day availability in response, before making a final call.
explanation: Option B is correct: the guardrail isn't moving generally, it's moving specifically among the exact population the boost created, same-day bookings, while advance bookings stay flat, which points directly at the boost itself as the mechanism. A same-day slot is easier to book impulsively and easier to blow off than one planned days ahead, so filling more of them is plausibly manufacturing lower-commitment bookings rather than capturing demand that was always going to show up. Providers bear the cost of a reserved slot going empty directly, in lost revenue and schedule disruption, so a guardrail moving this specifically in the newly-boosted segment isn't a cost to shrug off as generically expected. Option A treats the no-show increase as an undifferentiated, expected cost without engaging with the fact that it's concentrated exactly where the boost acted — that concentration is the signal the guardrail exists to catch, not background noise. Option C guesses at a specific cause, new patients, with no evidence given to support it, and doesn't address the actual, already-observed split, by booking lead time, that the data already shows. Option D delays the decision without a clear hypothesis for what two more weeks would reveal that the current same-day-versus-advance split hasn't already shown.
hints: The guardrail didn't move everywhere — it moved in one specific, newly-created segment. Ask what that concentration tells you about the mechanism.
Who bears the cost of a booked slot that goes unused, and does an easier way to book impulsively change how likely someone is to actually show up?

title: Stitch Fix's keep rate rose 6 points — but neither shipment type actually improved
scenario_context: Stitch Fix reports its platform-wide item keep rate, the share of shipped items a client purchases rather than returns, rose from 38% to 44% this quarter. Segmenting by shipment type: 'Fix Preview' shipments, where the client hand-picks some items themselves before a stylist fills the rest, held flat at 52% keep rate; traditional stylist-only 'Fix' shipments held flat at 34%. Fix Preview grew from 25% to 45% of all shipments this quarter after a deliberate push to launch it in more regions.
description: What's the most defensible read of the 44% platform-wide keep rate?
options: It's a mix-shift result, not a within-type improvement — both types held their own rate steady; Fix Preview is simply a bigger share of shipments now.
It's a genuine stylist-quality improvement — stylists are clearly getting better at picking items clients want to keep, reflected in the 6-point platform-wide rise.
The 44% figure is unreliable and shouldn't be reported at all, since blending two structurally different shipment types into one rate is never meaningful.
It's a partial improvement — the rise should be attributed half to the mix shift and half to genuine quality gains in both shipment types.
explanation: Option A is correct: this is a clean mix-shift read — both shipment types report the exact same keep rate this quarter as before, so none of the 6-point platform rise can be coming from either type getting better at picking items clients want. What changed is the blend: Fix Preview, which structurally keeps more because the client already chose some of the items themselves, nearly doubled its share of total shipments after a deliberate regional expansion. A blended average shifting toward a higher-performing type can rise even while every type's own rate is completely unchanged, and that's exactly what the segment cut shows here. Option B credits stylist quality with an improvement that the segment data explicitly rules out — stylist-only Fix shipments kept the identical 34% rate both quarters, so there's no quality signal to attribute anywhere in this result. Option C overcorrects; a blended rate isn't inherently meaningless, it's meaningful as a description of overall shipped-item outcomes, the issue is only in misattributing why it moved, not in reporting it at all. Option D splits the credit as though some real quality gain must be mixed in with the mix shift, but the segment data shows zero movement in either type's own rate — there's no quality-gain component to credit here, the entire 6 points is mix.
hints: Check whether each shipment type's own rate actually moved, or whether only the mix between the two types changed.
A blended rate can rise even when every group inside it stays exactly the same, if the mix shifts toward a group that structurally performs better. What changed about the mix this quarter?

title: Getaround's optional inspection — faster onboarding, a rising incident rate
scenario_context: Getaround tests relaxing its host vehicle-verification requirements (in-person inspection becomes optional for hosts with a clean 90-day rental history) to reduce onboarding friction for repeat hosts. Four weeks in: new host activations are up 22%, and time-to-first-booking for new hosts drops significantly. Safety incident reports, previously rare, involving cars with mechanical issues or undisclosed damage tick up specifically among hosts who skipped the now-optional inspection.
description: What's the most defensible strategic call?
options: Keep the relaxed policy — a 22% activation lift is a strong growth signal, and incident reports remain a small fraction of total rentals.
Revert to mandatory inspection for all hosts — the inspection was the safety backstop, and the risk isn't confined to any specific vehicle attribute.
Keep the optional-inspection path, but require it specifically for hosts whose listed vehicle is above a certain age or mileage threshold, where mechanical risk is highest.
Keep the relaxed policy, but add a mandatory post-rental damage-report survey to guests, treating detection after the fact as sufficient risk management.
explanation: Option B is correct: unlike a compliance or satisfaction metric where a narrow error can be scoped and contained, the in-person inspection here is the safety mechanism itself, and it was made optional broadly, not degraded in some narrow way — removing it is what's producing the incident increase, and nothing in the data ties the risk to a single identifiable vehicle attribute (age or mileage) rather than simply to skipped inspection in general. Getaround's entire trust claim rests on a guest being able to assume a listed vehicle isn't hiding a mechanical or damage problem, and reverting the inspection requirement is what restores the actual safety backstop, rather than a scoped compromise that leaves the mechanism gone for everyone else. Option A treats a physical-safety incident rate as background noise purely because of its current small share of total rentals, but the entire reason the inspection existed was to catch exactly this category of undisclosed problem before a guest ever drives the car — waving it off by its current size ignores that a mechanical or damage incident is a categorically different kind of cost than most guardrails this track evaluates. Option C sounds like a targeted, data-driven compromise, but nothing in the incident data ties the risk specifically to vehicle age or mileage rather than simply to skipping inspection itself — a newer, low-mileage car can just as easily hide undisclosed collision damage, so this scoping doesn't actually address the mechanism the audit flagged. Option D substitutes detection for prevention; a guest who already drove an unsafe or undisclosed-damage vehicle has already been exposed to the exact risk the inspection was meant to catch before the rental started.
hints: Ask whether the rising risk is genuinely tied to one identifiable vehicle attribute, or simply to whether inspection happened at all.
A physical-safety incident is a categorically different kind of cost than most guardrails — weigh what the inspection step was actually preventing, not just how small the incident count currently is.

title: Swiggy's Bangalore order drop — the analyst's same-day competitor verdict
scenario_context: Swiggy's order volume in Bangalore fell 11% over one week. An analyst reports: 'A competitor launched an aggressive discount campaign in Bangalore this week — that's obviously pulling our order share, we should respond with matching discounts immediately.' The recommendation is escalated to the city ops lead the same day.
description: What's the flaw in the analyst's conclusion?
options: The analyst identified a real competitive threat but proposed the wrong response; Swiggy should improve delivery speed instead of matching discounts.
The analyst didn't rule out simpler internal explanations, restaurant outages, delivery-partner shortages, app issues, before blaming a competitor.
There's no flaw — a competitor's aggressive discount campaign is a well-documented cause of order-volume drops, and the response is appropriately fast.
The flaw is comparing week-over-week instead of year-over-year, since Bangalore likely has strong seasonal order patterns.
explanation: Option B is correct: a MECE investigation checks the cheaper, internally-verifiable explanations before reaching for an external one that's harder to confirm and invites a costly response. Whether restaurant partners had unusual outages, whether delivery-partner supply was short in Bangalore that week, or whether the app itself had a local issue are all things Swiggy's own data can confirm or rule out quickly, and none of them were checked before the analyst jumped to a competitor's campaign — a real possibility, but not the only one, and not yet distinguished from the others. Committing to a discount-matching response before ruling out an internal, fixable cause risks spending real margin fighting a threat that may not even be the actual driver. Option A accepts the analyst's unverified external attribution and only critiques the proposed fix, but the deeper problem is that the cause itself was never actually confirmed — a different response to an unconfirmed cause is still built on the same unvalidated foundation. Option C takes a plausible external story at face value without requiring it be checked against simpler, internal explanations first, exactly the shortcut a structured diagnosis is built to catch. Option D raises a real general good practice, but it doesn't identify what's specifically wrong with the analyst's investigation here — the issue isn't the comparison window, it's that no MECE set of hypotheses was actually formed or tested before committing to a specific, costly response.
hints: The analyst reached for an external cause first. What simpler, internally-checkable explanations should typically be ruled out before that?
A real possibility isn't the same as a confirmed cause — what would distinguish this specific hypothesis from the other explanations that were never checked?

title: Handshake's fast-hire ranking boost — students convert more, small employers lose applicants
scenario_context: Handshake changes its job-recommendation ranking to prioritize postings from employers with a historically fast time-to-hire, reasoning that students are more likely to actually land a role from these postings. Four weeks in: student application-to-offer conversion is up 16% for postings shown, but the number of distinct employers a student sees in top recommendations drops from an average of 9 to 4, concentrated among large, fast-hiring employers; small and early-stage employers report a 30% drop in applicant volume.
description: What's the most defensible way to frame this trade-off?
options: This is a clear win for students — a 16% jump in conversion means students are getting hired more often, which is the platform's core value proposition.
This is a clear loss for the platform — small employers are a core part of Handshake's supply side, so the ranking change should revert immediately.
Name the two-sided trade-off — students landing roles faster is real, but it risks starving the smaller-employer supply Handshake also needs.
Reframe success around total postings viewed platform-wide, since that better reflects marketplace activity than either conversion or employer diversity.
explanation: Option C is correct: Handshake's value to students depends on a healthy, varied employer base actually posting and hiring, not just on students who land roles at whichever employers already hire fastest. The conversion lift for students who see these postings is a real win, but it's coming at a structural cost to the marketplace's other side: a 30% drop in applicant volume for small and early-stage employers threatens their reason to keep posting at all, and a platform that loses that supply narrows what students who don't fit the fast-hiring-employer mold can even find. Naming both halves, the real student-side win and the real supply-side risk, is what a two-sided marketplace result actually calls for. Option A isolates the metric the change targeted and calls it an unqualified win, but a recommendation system that boosts conversion by concentrating outcomes among a shrinking set of employers is trading breadth for a narrower kind of success, not simply succeeding. Option B swings to an immediate full reversal based on the supply-side cost alone, discarding a real, meaningful improvement in how well students who see these postings are converting, without weighing whether a blended or capped ranking approach could address the supply concern while keeping some of the win. Option D introduces a metric, postings viewed, that isn't evidenced as connected to either side's actual outcome in the scenario, and swapping the yardstick sidesteps the trade-off already visible in the four weeks of results rather than confronting it.
hints: This is a two-sided marketplace — a ranking change that helps one side's outcome can threaten the other side's willingness to participate at all. Look for the option naming both.
One number moved because of what the ranking rewards directly; another moved because of who got squeezed out. Check whether they're connected before picking a single winner.

title: Loom's auto-copy link — predicting which funnel step actually moves
scenario_context: Loom changes its recording flow so that finishing a recording automatically copies the shareable link to the clipboard, removing the separate step where users previously had to click a 'Copy Link' button after recording. The team's hypothesis is that this specifically removes friction from the moment right after recording ends, without changing anything about how viewers who receive a link behave once they click it.
description: If this hypothesis is correct, which funnel step should show the biggest immediate change, and which should stay essentially unaffected?
options: The share-rate from 'recording completed' to 'link sent' should rise the most; the view-rate to 'video watched' should stay flat.
The view-rate from 'link received' to 'video watched' should rise the most, since a link that's easier to send is also a link people are more motivated to watch.
Both the share rate and the view rate should rise by comparable amounts, since removing any friction earlier in the flow tends to lift every step downstream proportionally.
Recording completion rate itself should rise, since users are more likely to finish recording when they know sharing afterward will be effortless.
explanation: Option A is correct: the change acts on exactly one moment, the instant after recording ends, by removing a manual copy step, so the step immediately downstream of that moment, whether a completed recording actually gets shared with someone, is where the direct, mechanical effect should show up first and most. The hypothesis explicitly states nothing changes about viewer behavior once a link is received, so the view-rate step, which depends entirely on the recipient's own decision to click and watch, has no mechanism in this change to move at all. Option B predicts the change ripples forward into recipient behavior, but nothing about how a link was copied should affect a viewer's motivation to click it, that step is downstream of a moment the change never touches. Option C assumes friction removed at one step automatically lifts every later step proportionally, but that's not how a funnel works when the friction removed is specific to one exact action, a viewer receiving a link has no visibility into how easy or hard it was for the sender to copy it, so there's no reason their click-through behavior would shift at all. Option D reaches upstream of the change entirely, recording completion happens before the copy-link moment even occurs, so a change to what happens after recording ends has no plausible mechanism to affect whether someone finishes recording in the first place.
hints: The change acts on one specific moment in the flow. Ask which funnel step sits immediately downstream of that exact moment, and which steps sit before or two steps removed from it.
A viewer who receives a link has no way of knowing how that link was copied. Would anything about their own decision to click actually change?

title: Wag!'s on-time arrival tap — a self-report walkers can submit early
scenario_context: Wag! ranks dog walkers in search results partly by on-time arrival rate, self-reported via an 'I've arrived' button the walker taps on their phone. Trust & safety finds a cluster of walkers tapping 'arrived' while still blocks away, sometimes minutes before actually reaching the client's door, then walking the dog for a shorter time than booked. The team wants an arrival signal that isn't just a self-report.
description: Which candidate signal is most resistant to being reported early rather than actually true?
options: Keep the self-reported arrival tap, but require walkers to also submit a photo of the client's front door at arrival.
Replace on-time arrival rate with average client star rating, since dissatisfied clients will naturally rate late walkers lower.
Keep the self-reported tap, but add a warning that falsifying arrival time is against Wag!'s terms of service.
Use the phone's GPS at the moment of the tap to confirm the walker is actually near the client's address before it counts as on-time.
explanation: Option D is correct: cross-checking the self-report against an independent, harder-to-fake signal, the phone's actual GPS position at the moment of the tap, closes the specific gap being exploited. A walker can still tap the button whenever they want, but the tap only counts as a valid on-time arrival if the device's location data agrees they were actually near the client's address, which a walker blocks away can't manufacture without also being physically closer. Option A's photo idea sounds like independent verification, but a photo can be taken from a distance with a zoom, taken early and held, or even reused from a prior visit to the same address, it doesn't actually confirm the walker was there at the reported time. Option B swaps in a different metric that's driven by many factors beyond punctuality, a walker could arrive on time but still get a low rating for something unrelated, or arrive late but get a good rating anyway if the client didn't notice, so it doesn't isolate the specific behavior, false arrival reporting, the team is trying to catch. Option C adds a policy warning with no technical verification behind it at all; a warning doesn't change whether the walker's tap is actually true, it only threatens a consequence that requires already knowing it's false to enforce.
hints: Ask what a walker who wants to report early would need to fake, and whether each candidate actually requires something they can't fake.
A self-report resists gaming only when it's checked against a second, independent signal the person making the report doesn't fully control.

title: Warby Parker's virtual try-on — conversion up, and the guardrail moved the right way too
scenario_context: Warby Parker ships a virtual try-on AR feature letting shoppers preview glasses on their own face via phone camera before buying. Four-week test: purchase conversion is up 12% among shoppers who use the feature. The guardrail the team pre-registered, return rate for 'doesn't suit my face' reasons, is actually lower for AR-try-on purchasers (8%) than for shoppers who bought without using it (14%), and no other guardrail moved.
description: What's the most defensible call?
options: Ship to 100% — conversion is up and the pre-registered guardrail moved in the favorable direction, suggesting the feature is helping people pick frames that actually suit them.
Hold the rollout — a 12% conversion lift this large this early is almost always a novelty effect that will fade within a few weeks.
Ship only to first-time Warby Parker shoppers, since returning customers already know what suits them and don't need the feature.
Extend the test — an 8% versus 14% return-rate gap needs a larger sample before it can be trusted as a real difference.
explanation: Option A is correct: this is the case where the guardrail the team specifically pre-registered to catch a plausible downside, more returns from people who bought based on an inaccurate virtual preview, moved in the favorable direction instead; purchasers who used the feature return for fit-related reasons less often than purchasers who didn't. That's consistent with the feature doing exactly what it's meant to do, helping shoppers make a more informed choice before buying, rather than trading conversion for a hidden cost. With the primary metric up and the one guardrail that mattered here moving the right way, there's no signal left in the data pointing toward caution. Option B asserts a novelty-effect concern with nothing in the scenario supporting it; conversion features rooted in giving people better information before a purchase decision, rather than in a shiny new interaction, aren't the class of change where novelty decay is the default assumption, and no week-over-week decay is mentioned here at all. Option C proposes scoping the launch to a segment for a plausible-sounding but unstated reason, but there's no evidence given that returning customers behave any differently, restricting the launch this way discards value for a population the data hasn't shown any problem with. Option D calls for a bigger sample on the guardrail specifically, but the return-rate gap is a large, directionally favorable difference, not a marginal or concerning one, asking to wait longer with no stated concern about the sample's reliability treats caution as free when the data in hand already tells a coherent, positive story.
hints: Check what direction the team's own pre-registered guardrail actually moved, not just whether the primary metric looks good.
A guardrail moving in the favorable direction is different from a guardrail that simply didn't move. What does that difference tell you about whether to look for more caution?

title: Redfin's page-view spike — the analyst's early-spring verdict
scenario_context: Redfin's daily listing-page view count jumped 35% starting on a Tuesday, with no marketing change or new listings driving it. An analyst reports: 'This is a genuine surge in buyer interest, probably seasonal — spring house-hunting is starting early this year. No further investigation needed.'
description: What's the flaw in the analyst's conclusion?
options: There's no flaw — a sudden 35% jump with a plausible seasonal story is sufficient grounds to close the investigation.
The flaw is that seasonal patterns should be measured year-over-year, not compared to the analyst's general impression of when spring house-hunting starts.
The analyst should have consulted the marketing team before writing any conclusion, since marketing owns all traffic-driving initiatives.
The analyst never checked whether the traffic increase is real, unique visitors or a spike in automated bot traffic, a distinct, checkable explanation.
explanation: Option D is correct: a sudden, single-day step-change in page views, with no marketing change and no new listings to explain it, is exactly the shape that should prompt a bot-traffic or scraping check before any behavioral story is accepted — real seasonal shifts in buyer interest typically build gradually over days or weeks, they don't usually appear as a sharp jump starting on one specific day. Checking whether the increase is concentrated in unique authenticated sessions versus anonymous, high-frequency requests hitting the same listings repeatedly is a fast, checkable step the analyst skipped entirely in favor of a plausible-sounding narrative. Option A accepts a plausible story with no verification at all, exactly the shortcut a structured investigation is meant to catch, a jump this sudden deserves at least one basic check before being called genuine. Option B raises a reasonable general point about seasonal comparisons, but it doesn't identify the more fundamental gap, whether the traffic is even real visitors at all, a better seasonal comparison wouldn't resolve that question. Option C reaches for a process fix, consulting another team, that doesn't itself investigate anything; the analyst can and should check the traffic composition directly before looping anyone else in.
hints: A sudden, single-day jump with no known cause has more than one explanation. What distinguishes real visitor interest from something else generating the same page-view count?
Real behavioral shifts tend to build gradually. What does a sharp, single-day step change usually suggest is worth checking first?

title: Talkspace's Quick Match — faster sessions, weaker fit
scenario_context: Talkspace tests a 'Quick Match' flow that auto-assigns a new user to any available therapist within 2 hours, replacing a preference-based matching questionnaire that took an average of 3 days. Sign-up-to-first-session completion rises from 61% to 79%. But among Quick Match users, self-reported therapist fit ('I feel understood by my therapist') after session 1 is 11 points lower than among questionnaire-matched users, and therapist-switch requests within the first month are roughly double.
description: What's the most defensible strategic call?
options: Ship Quick Match to 100% — the completion-rate gain is large and getting more people into any session at all is the primary goal of a mental-health product.
Revert to the questionnaire-only flow entirely — a therapy product's core promise is fit and trust, and Quick Match is measurably degrading both.
Keep Quick Match as the default for speed, but run the same brief preference questionnaire in parallel and use it to assign within the pool of therapists available in that 2-hour window.
Ship Quick Match only to users who've never used therapy before, since new-to-therapy users are less likely to have strong preferences about fit anyway.
explanation: Option C is correct: the two things Talkspace is actually trading against each other, speed to a first session and the fit that makes a session valuable, aren't fundamentally incompatible, they were just bundled as an either/or in the original test design. Running the brief preference signal in parallel and matching within whichever therapists are available in the fast window keeps almost all of the completion-rate gain, since it doesn't reintroduce the 3-day wait, while directly addressing the mechanism behind the fit drop, assignment that ignores preference entirely. This is the option that treats the trade-off as a design problem to solve rather than a side to pick. Option A treats getting into any session as sufficient, but a therapy product's actual value depends on the therapeutic relationship working, and a near-doubling of first-month switch requests is direct evidence that a meaningful share of Quick Match users aren't getting a session that's actually working for them, a session happening isn't the same as the product delivering its value. Option B swings to a full reversion, discarding a large, genuine access improvement, getting people into care in hours instead of days plausibly matters most for someone in acute distress, without first checking whether a hybrid design could preserve that access gain. Option D's new-user-only scoping rests on an unsupported assumption, that people new to therapy don't have preferences that matter to fit, nothing in the scenario suggests fit matters less for first-time therapy users, if anything a bad first experience could be more consequential for someone deciding whether therapy works for them at all.
hints: The two things trading off here aren't necessarily mutually exclusive. Ask whether a design exists that keeps most of one gain while addressing the mechanism behind the other's loss.

One guardrail here isn't just a number, it's a proxy for whether the product's core promise, a relationship that actually helps, is being delivered. Weigh what a rising switch-request rate is telling you.

title: Steam's refund rate rose 3 points — concentrated where volume also grew
scenario_context: Steam's platform-wide refund rate (refund requests within the 2-hour/14-day policy window, as a share of purchases) rose from 6% to 9% over the past month. A breakdown by game genre shows the increase concentrated almost entirely in early-access titles, where refund rate jumped from 11% to 22%; refund rates for fully-released titles are flat at 4%. Early-access titles also grew from 9% to 16% of total purchases this month after a platform-wide 'Early Access Spotlight' merchandising push.
description: What's the most defensible next step?
options: Report the platform-wide 9% refund rate as a meaningful decline in purchase quality and investigate the checkout flow for bugs.
Ignore the genre breakdown, since a refund is a refund regardless of what kind of game it came from, and the aggregate number is what matters to finance.
Focus on early access titles, where both the rate and volume increases concentrate, and check why the spotlighted titles are refunding more.
Recommend removing early-access titles from the Spotlight program entirely, since the refund-rate math clearly shows they're a worse purchase for consumers.
explanation: Option C is correct: the segment cut has already done the diagnostic work — both the rate itself (11% to 22%) and the volume of purchases in that category (9% to 16% of all purchases) moved specifically in early access, while fully-released titles stayed completely flat. That double-movement in the same segment is a strong, specific lead: something about the spotlighted early-access titles, whether they're less complete than typical early-access norms, more aggressively marketed, or simply getting more first-time-genre buyers who don't know what to expect, is worth checking directly, rather than treating the platform number as one undifferentiated signal. Option A treats the 9% platform-wide number as the object of investigation and points at checkout, but nothing in the segment data suggests a checkout problem; the entire movement is explained by one specific, identifiable category behaving differently, chasing a generic technical cause ignores the lead already in hand. Option B refuses to use the one piece of information that actually explains the movement, a refund's business impact may be uniform, but understanding why refunds rose specifically requires looking at where they're concentrated, dismissing that as irrelevant throws away the diagnosis. Option D jumps to a specific operational recommendation, pulling early access from the merchandising program entirely, before actually confirming what about this batch of spotlighted titles is driving the elevated rate, a much bigger swing than the data yet supports without first checking the mechanism.
hints: Two things moved together in the same specific category. Check what that category is before deciding whether the platform-wide number itself is the thing to investigate.

A segment where both the volume and the rate increased at once is a stronger lead than a platform-wide average. What would you check about that specific segment before recommending any operational change?

title: Deel's self-serve onboarding — faster payments, a compliance gap in three countries
scenario_context: Deel tests a self-serve compliance flow that lets new customers onboard contractors in a new country without a compliance specialist reviewing the paperwork first, cutting time-to-first-payment from 6 days to 1 day. Onboarding completion rises 24%. Compliance audits of the self-serve flow find a 4% rate of misclassified worker status (contractor vs. employee) in three specific countries with unusually complex labor rules, versus under 0.5% in the specialist-reviewed flow across the same three countries.
description: What's the most defensible way to frame this trade-off?
options: Name the trade-off by jurisdiction — keep self-serve for most countries where misclassification risk is low, and require specialist review specifically for the three complex-rule countries.
This is a clear win — a 24% onboarding lift and faster payments are the core value proposition, and a 4% misclassification rate is a small fraction of all onboarded contractors.
This is a clear loss — worker misclassification carries real legal and financial exposure, so self-serve onboarding should be reverted entirely across all countries.
Keep self-serve everywhere, but add a disclaimer that customers are solely responsible for correct worker classification, shifting legal exposure to them.
explanation: Option A is correct: the risk isn't spread evenly, it's concentrated in three specific countries with unusually complex labor rules, while the self-serve flow works fine, at under 0.5% misclassification just like the specialist flow, everywhere else. Scoping the fix to exactly where the risk lives keeps the real onboarding-speed win for the large majority of countries while closing the specific gap the audit found, rather than treating the whole global flow as one indivisible decision. Option B treats a 4% misclassification rate as small in isolation, but worker misclassification is a compliance and legal exposure issue, for both Deel and its customers, not a minor quality blemish, and a rate 8x higher than the specialist-reviewed baseline in the exact same countries is a specific, identified gap, not background noise to average away. Option C swings to a full global reversion, discarding a real and substantial onboarding win in the large majority of countries where the self-serve flow is performing just as well as specialist review, a broader response than the country-specific pattern in the audit actually supports. Option D tries to solve a compliance accuracy problem with a liability disclaimer, but shifting who's legally responsible doesn't reduce the actual rate of misclassification happening, or the underlying legal risk in jurisdictions with genuinely complex rules, a customer accepting liability doesn't make the classification correct.
hints: The risk isn't the same everywhere — check where the audit actually found the gap before deciding whether the whole global flow needs to change.
A rate that looks small in isolation can still be a specific, identified compliance gap. Compare it to the same countries' baseline under the other flow, not just to the global average.

title: Sephora's Beauty Insider spend gap — the auto-enroll proposal
scenario_context: Sephora's data team finds that Beauty Insider loyalty members spend 3.2x more per year than non-members. A marketing lead proposes: 'Let's auto-enroll every new customer into the loyalty program at checkout instead of requiring opt-in, since loyalty membership clearly drives higher spend, and this should lift average customer spend across the board.'
description: What's the flaw in the marketing lead's reasoning?
options: There's no flaw — a 3.2x spend difference is a large, statistically meaningful gap, and auto-enrollment is a low-cost way to capture that lift.
The flaw is measurement, not causation; Sephora should verify the 3.2x figure using a different attribution window before acting on it.
Auto-enrollment will work, but only after Sephora also improves the loyalty program's point-redemption options to give new members a reason to spend more.
Customers who opted into loyalty are plausibly already more engaged, higher-spend shoppers — membership may reflect that pattern, not cause it.
explanation: Option D is correct: this is the classic self-selection trap — people who actively seek out and opt into a loyalty program are plausibly the customers who already shop at Sephora frequently and spend more, being the kind of shopper who signs up for a rewards program and being a high-spend shopper likely share a common cause, rather than one causing the other. Auto-enrolling every customer, including plenty who were never going to be high-spend shoppers regardless of membership status, gives no reason to expect the same 3.2x gap to appear for that much broader, unselected population. Option A treats the size and statistical strength of the observed gap as proof of causation, but a large, robust correlation is still a correlation, the self-selection explanation is fully consistent with an even bigger, more reliably-measured 3.2x gap. Option B redirects to a measurement concern, a different attribution window, that doesn't address the actual flaw in the reasoning, whether membership causes spend or merely correlates with a pre-existing spending pattern, a cleaner measurement of the same observational comparison wouldn't resolve that. Option C accepts the causal claim and proposes an enhancement on top of it, skipping past the core issue entirely, that the original 3.2x figure was never established as caused by membership in the first place, so building further plans on it doesn't fix the flaw.
hints: The people already in the loyalty program got there by choosing to join. Ask what kind of shopper tends to make that choice in the first place.
A trait and an outcome can share a common cause without either one causing the other. What might make someone both more likely to opt in and more likely to already spend more?

title: Opendoor's offer-accuracy metric — the lowball that would look like a win
scenario_context: Opendoor's algorithmic home-offer team is evaluated partly on 'offer accuracy,' how close the initial cash offer is to the eventual resale price. A regional lead proposes rewarding offer teams for improving this metric. An analyst flags that a team can trivially improve offer accuracy by systematically lowballing every offer by 8-10%, since a consistently low offer is easy to land close to on the resale side — this would look like an accuracy win while actually making Opendoor's offers less competitive and hurting seller acceptance rates.
description: Which candidate metric change would make offer accuracy resistant to being gamed by systematic lowballing?
options: Keep offer accuracy as the sole metric, but require regional leads to sign off on any offer more than 10% below the algorithm's raw estimate.
Replace offer accuracy with seller acceptance rate alone, since a metric sellers actually respond to can't be gamed by an internal pricing choice.
Pair offer accuracy with seller acceptance rate, so a team can only improve one by sacrificing the other, closing off lowballing as a free win.
Keep offer accuracy, but only measure it on homes that eventually sell within 60 days, filtering out slower, harder-to-price properties.
explanation: Option C is correct: pairing the two metrics makes the gaming move self-defeating. Systematic lowballing can still push offer accuracy up, but sellers who receive a worse offer than they'd get from a competing cash buyer are less likely to accept it, so seller acceptance rate falls in direct response — a team chasing better accuracy through lowballing pays for it immediately on the other number, and the two together only both rise if offers are genuinely getting more accurate at a price sellers still find competitive. Option A adds a review step but leaves the accuracy metric itself untouched and gameable, a team can still lowball within whatever threshold triggers sign-off, and sign-off itself doesn't verify why the offer was set low, just that someone approved it. Option B swaps to a single different metric, but a metric evaluated alone is still vulnerable to its own gaming vector, a team could chase acceptance rate by simply overpaying on every offer, trading the original gaming risk for a new, opposite one rather than closing the hole. Option D's filtering idea addresses which homes count, not the actual lowballing incentive, a team could still lowball freely on the homes that do qualify within 60 days, the fix doesn't touch the mechanism the analyst flagged at all.
hints: Ask what a team could do for free, without any real pricing skill, to move the metric, and whether each candidate still rewards that move.
A metric resists gaming when the same tactic that inflates it also costs something on a second, connected number.

title: Indeed's new ranking algo — more applications, weaker matches
scenario_context: Indeed tests a new job-ranking algorithm that prioritizes postings likely to get a fast application after viewing. Two-week result: applications submitted per job view rise 19%. But employer-reported application quality ('candidates who meet the basic listed requirements') drops from 71% to 54%, and employer subscription-renewal intent, surveyed at contract end, falls 8 points specifically among employers who received the new ranking.
description: What's the most defensible call?
options: Ship to 100% — a 19% rise in applications per view is a strong top-line win for the marketplace's core action.
Ship, but only measure success by applications per view going forward, since that's the metric the algorithm change directly targeted.
Extend the test — an 8-point renewal-intent drop is a survey measure, not actual churn, and needs to be validated against real renewal data before it means anything.
Hold the rollout — more unqualified applications are eroding what employers actually pay Indeed for, and it's already showing in their stated intent to leave.
explanation: Option D is correct: Indeed's employer customers pay for qualified applicants, not raw application volume, so a change that drives more applications while cutting the share who meet basic requirements nearly in half is degrading the actual product employers are buying, and that degradation is already visible in the employers' own stated intent to not renew. A rising top-line action metric that's directly connected to a falling customer-value signal on the paying side of the marketplace is a compound result pointing the same direction, not two separate things to weigh against each other. Option A treats the application-volume metric as the win condition on its own, but volume was never actually the thing Indeed's employer customers pay for, it's a proxy that this test result shows can rise while the underlying value falls. Option B commits to permanently tracking only the metric the algorithm was built to move, locking in exactly the blind spot this test just exposed, once a metric known to trade off against employer value becomes the only thing measured, that trade-off becomes invisible going forward. Option C is right that a survey signal is softer than realized churn, but dismissing it as unreliable ignores that it's directly consistent with a large, hard, already-measured quality drop, the survey isn't the only evidence here, it's corroborating evidence for a mechanism already visible in the requirements-met rate.
hints: Ask who actually pays Indeed and what they're paying for — is it application volume, or something volume alone doesn't guarantee?
Two of these signals may be telling the same story rather than two separate ones. Check whether the quality drop and the renewal-intent drop are connected.

title: Vrbo's late-shown fees — clicks up, checkout abandonment up too
scenario_context: Vrbo tests displaying only the nightly base rate in search results, moving cleaning fees and the guest service fee to appear for the first time at checkout, instead of showing an all-in estimated total upfront. Search-result click-through rises 15%. But checkout-page abandonment, once the full price including fees is shown, rises from 22% to 34%, and post-stay reviews mentioning 'hidden fees' or 'surprise costs' roughly triple.
description: What's the most defensible way to frame this result?
options: Name the trade-off — clicks are up, but so are abandonment and fee complaints; completed, trusted bookings aren't clear from click-through alone.
This is a clear win — a 15% click-through lift is a strong top-of-funnel signal, and checkout abandonment is a normal part of any booking flow.
This is a clear loss — hidden fees are always a bad practice, so Vrbo should immediately revert to showing all-in pricing in search results.
Ship the change, but add a small 'fees may apply' disclaimer text under the search-result price, treating disclosure as sufficient without changing what's shown.
explanation: Option A is correct: the three numbers that moved here aren't telling one simple story, they're describing a shift in where the same friction shows up and what it costs. More people click in because the sticker-shock moment moved later, but a meaningfully larger share now bounce at checkout once they see the real price, and the guests who push through anyway are leaving a lot more complaints about being surprised, a trust cost that a review-reading future guest will also see. Whether completed, trusted bookings, the thing that actually matters, went up or down isn't answerable from the click-through number in isolation, that's exactly why naming the shape of the trade-off, rather than picking a side from one metric, is the defensible move. Option B isolates the metric the change was designed to move and calls it a win, but a rising top-of-funnel number funded by a bigger drop-off later in the same funnel plus a tripling of complaints isn't obviously a win, it's a redistribution of the same friction with an added trust cost. Option C treats the practice as categorically disqualifying and calls for an immediate full reversion without weighing what was actually gained, three numbers moved, not one, and a reversion decision should engage with all three rather than the fee-disclosure question alone. Option D tries to solve a substantive pricing-transparency problem with a small disclaimer, but the abandonment and complaint data are about guests encountering the real price late, not about whether they were warned fees might exist, a vague disclaimer doesn't change when the actual number appears.
hints: Three numbers moved here, and they may not all be pointing toward one clean verdict. Ask what happened to the friction, not just where it now shows up in the funnel.
A rising top-of-funnel metric funded by a much larger drop-off later, plus a trust cost showing up in reviews, isn't automatically a win. What would you need to know before calling it one?

title: Zwift's ride-completion drop — the analyst blames the new climb
scenario_context: Zwift's average ride-completion rate (share of started rides finished without early exit) fell from 88% to 79% over two weeks, right after a new route, 'Alpe du Zwift,' a notoriously long, difficult climb, was added to the featured rotation. An analyst reports: 'Riders are quitting because the new featured route is too hard — we should remove it from the featured rotation immediately.'
description: What's the flaw in the analyst's conclusion?
options: The flaw is that difficulty is subjective; Zwift should survey riders directly about whether they found the route too hard instead of inferring it from completion rate.
There's no flaw — a route this difficult being added right before the drop is decisive evidence, and pulling it is the obviously correct response.
The analyst should first consult the route-design team before making any recommendation, since they own decisions about the featured rotation.
The analyst never checked whether the drop concentrates among riders who chose the new route, versus a platform-wide drop unrelated to it.
explanation: Option D is correct: 'featured' doesn't mean every rider who started a ride that week rode this specific route, some meaningful share chose other routes entirely, so the first, cheap check is whether the completion-rate drop is concentrated among riders who actually selected Alpe du Zwift, versus spread evenly across riders regardless of which route they picked. If the drop is isolated to that route's own completion rate while other routes are unaffected, the difficulty hypothesis holds up; if completion fell platform-wide including on easy, unrelated routes, something else, unrelated to this one route, is going on, and pulling the featured route wouldn't fix it. Option A raises a real alternative measurement, but it doesn't identify the actual gap in the analyst's reasoning, which is a missing segmentation check, not a preference for survey data over completion-rate data. Option B accepts a timing coincidence and a plausible mechanism as decisive, exactly the shortcut a structured diagnosis exists to catch, especially before recommending an operational change. Option C proposes a process step, looping in another team, that doesn't itself investigate anything, the segmentation check is something the analyst can and should run directly before recommending any change to the rotation.
hints: 'Featured' doesn't mean everyone rode it. What's the first, cheap check that would confirm whether the drop is actually tied to this specific route?
If the difficulty hypothesis is right, the drop should look very different for riders who picked the new route versus riders who picked something else. Has that split been checked?

title: GoodRx's auto-recommended pharmacy — priced by cash, ranked partly by revenue share
scenario_context: GoodRx tests an 'auto-recommended pharmacy' badge shown by default on drug search results, chosen by a blended score that weighs both the cash price at that pharmacy and the revenue-share GoodRx earns from that pharmacy partner. In 18% of searches, the auto-recommended pharmacy is not the single lowest cash price available, though it's within a few dollars. Click-through to the recommended pharmacy rises sharply versus the old plain price-sorted list.
description: What's the most defensible strategic call?
options: Keep the blended score — GoodRx is a business, and factoring in partner revenue share alongside price is a reasonable way to run a marketplace.
Keep the blended score, but only show it for searches where the recommended pharmacy is within $5 of the lowest price, on the reasoning that small differences don't matter to consumers.
Drop revenue-share from the ranking and sort strictly by lowest cash price; let partner terms show up in placement, not in what's labeled 'recommended.'
Keep the current design, but add a small text label disclosing that the recommendation considers partner terms, treating disclosure as sufficient without changing the ranking itself.
explanation: Option C is correct: GoodRx's entire reason to exist for a user is trust that the price it surfaces is genuinely the best one findable, once the ranking itself is shaped by what GoodRx earns rather than purely by what the user pays, the core promise is compromised regardless of how small the gap looks in any single search. Separating the two, rank strictly on price, and let partner economics show up in layout or promotion rather than in which pharmacy gets called out as 'recommended', keeps the one signal users actually rely on honest while still leaving room for GoodRx's business relationships to exist elsewhere on the page. Option A accepts a revenue-influenced ranking as an ordinary business trade-off, but a price-comparison tool's entire value proposition is that its top recommendation is the best deal, not the best deal after also serving GoodRx's own economics, that's a different and more corrosive kind of trade-off than a typical marketplace ranking choice. Option B tries to bound the harm with a dollar threshold, but it doesn't remove the conflict of interest, it just decides how much of a user's money GoodRx is willing to quietly cost them before the practice becomes unacceptable, an arbitrary line rather than a principled fix. Option D treats disclosure as equivalent to fixing the ranking, but a small label doesn't change that most users, especially anyone in a time-pressured moment like filling a prescription, will trust the default 'recommended' badge rather than independently re-checking every price on the page.
hints: Ask what GoodRx's core promise to a user actually is, and whether a ranking shaped partly by what GoodRx earns is compatible with that promise, however small the price gap looks in any one case.

A dollar threshold and a disclosure label both leave the underlying conflict of interest in place. Is there a version of this that keeps the business relationship without touching what gets called 'recommended'?

title: Toptal's stricter vetting bar — predicting the retention curve's shape
scenario_context: Toptal tightens its freelancer vetting process, raising the bar so only the top 3% of applicants pass, down from roughly 8% previously. The team's hypothesis is that this raises the average quality of freelancers clients are matched with, which should improve client retention specifically by reducing the 'bad match, client churns after one project' failure mode, without necessarily changing how many total freelancers are available to match against.
description: If this hypothesis is correct, what should happen to the shape of the client Day-30-through-Day-180 retention curve for post-change client cohorts compared to pre-change cohorts?
options: The whole curve should shift higher only in the very first 30 days, since a better first match mainly affects a client's very first impression.
The curve should be unaffected in shape, but clients should complete projects faster, since higher-quality freelancers work more efficiently.
The curve should dip lower initially, since a smaller pool of vetted freelancers means noticeably longer wait times to get matched, which could hurt early retention.
The early drop-off after a client's first project should shrink, raising the curve's later plateau, since fewer clients churn from a bad first match.
explanation: Option D is correct: the hypothesis specifically targets one failure mode, clients churning after a single bad-match project, so the expected signature is a smaller early drop-off, the exact place that failure mode shows up in a retention curve, which mechanically raises where the curve settles later on, since fewer clients are being lost to that specific cause before they'd otherwise have stuck around. This isn't a general uplift to the whole curve or a single-point change, it's a change to the shape of the early decline specifically. Option A predicts a Day-30-only shift, but retaining a client for the first month doesn't guarantee they stay through Day-180, if the mechanism is genuinely fewer bad-match churns, that effect should persist in a higher plateau rather than being confined to the very first window. Option B predicts faster project completion instead of a retention effect, but the hypothesis is specifically about match quality reducing churn, not about freelancer working speed, nothing in the premise supports a completion-time claim at all. Option C introduces a new negative effect, longer wait times from a smaller vetted pool, that isn't part of the stated hypothesis and isn't supported by anything given, if wait times did lengthen that would be a separate, competing effect to consider, but it's not what this specific hypothesis predicts.
hints: The hypothesis names one specific failure mode being reduced. Ask where in a retention curve that particular failure mode would normally show up.
A change to one specific cause of early churn should show up as a change in the curve's shape in that exact window, not as a uniform lift everywhere or a change to an unrelated metric.

title: Lime's ride-completion drop — two cities, one firmware update, one ticket pattern
scenario_context: Lime's platform-wide ride-completion rate (rides ended normally vs. ended by a support ticket or app error) fell from 96% to 91% over 10 days. A city-by-city breakdown shows the drop concentrated entirely in two cities that received a firmware update to scooter GPS units on the same day the metric started falling; every other city's completion rate is unchanged. The two affected cities' support tickets show a spike specifically in 'ride wouldn't end / GPS stuck' complaints.
description: What's the most defensible read?
options: The drop is likely a real, narrow artifact of the firmware update — it matches the two affected cities, the exact ship day, and a GPS-stuck ticket pattern.
The drop reflects a genuine behavior change among riders in those two cities, and the firmware timing is a coincidence worth noting but not confirming.
The drop should be treated as platform-wide until proven otherwise, since a 5-point completion-rate decline is too large to attribute to just two cities.
The support-ticket spike is unrelated noise; completion rate and support tickets measure different things and shouldn't be reasoned about together.
explanation: Option A is correct: three separate pieces of evidence line up on the same explanation — the geographic concentration matches exactly the two cities that got the update, the timing matches the exact day it shipped, and the support-ticket content, GPS stuck, rides not ending, directly describes the mechanism by which a GPS or connectivity issue would prevent a ride from ending normally and instead route it to a support ticket or error state. This isn't a single coincidental data point, it's a converging pattern across location, timing, and complaint content all pointing at the same technical cause. Option B calls the firmware timing a coincidence 'worth noting but not confirming,' but dismissing this much converging evidence, exact cities, exact day, and a mechanism-matching complaint pattern, understates what's already been established here, this is closer to confirmed than merely suggestive. Option C insists on treating the drop as platform-wide despite direct evidence it's isolated to two cities, the concentration is the finding, not something to override by defaulting to the platform-wide number because the overall decline sounds large.
