Option D artificially separates two signals that are describing the same underlying event, a GPS malfunction would mechanically both prevent normal ride-ending and generate exactly the support tickets observed, treating them as unrelated ignores the shared mechanism connecting them.
hints: Three different kinds of evidence point at the same explanation here — geography, timing, and complaint content. Check whether they're converging or actually independent.
A support ticket describing the exact mechanism that would explain a metric's drop is stronger evidence than a coincidence. Weigh what the ticket content is actually telling you.

title: Brex's 'active customer' growth — the mid-quarter definition change
scenario_context: Brex reports 'active customers' grew 34% this quarter, a number highlighted in its board deck as evidence of accelerating adoption. A finance analyst discovers the definition of 'active' changed mid-quarter from 'completed at least one transaction in the last 30 days' to 'has at least one card issued to an employee,' a much lower bar that doesn't require any actual spending activity.
description: What's the most defensible way to characterize the 34% growth figure?
options: It's a legitimate growth number — more issued cards is still evidence Brex is being adopted by more companies, regardless of transaction activity.
It's understated, if anything — companies with issued but unused cards are very likely to start transacting soon, so the true adoption number is probably higher.
It should be reported net of the definition change, subtracting exactly the accounts that would have failed the old bar, to isolate the real number.
It's not comparable to prior quarters at all — the new, looser definition mixes real growth with a denominator that just got easier to qualify for.
explanation: Option D is correct: 'active customers' is used as a growth metric specifically because it's supposed to signal companies actually using the product, and changing the qualifying bar mid-quarter from real transaction activity to a much lower one, simply having a card issued, means this quarter's count and every prior quarter's count are answering two different questions. Some real share of the 34% may reflect genuine new adoption, but an unknown share is just accounts that would have failed the old, stricter bar now clearing the new, looser one, and there's no way to separate the two from the headline number alone. Reporting it as straightforward growth compares two differently-defined populations as if they were the same metric. Option A accepts issued-but-unused cards as meaningful adoption evidence, but the entire reason 'active' historically required a transaction was to distinguish companies actually using Brex from companies that merely signed up, dropping that bar erases the distinction the metric was built to make. Option B assumes unused cards will convert to real usage soon, an assumption stated with no supporting evidence in the scenario, and even if some do convert, that's a claim about the future, not a defense of counting them as already active today. Option C proposes a real fix in spirit, but doing it requires actually recomputing this quarter's count under the old, stricter definition, not just reporting the current number 'net of' an unspecified adjustment, the fix has to be a recalculation, not a caveat.
hints: Check whether this quarter's number and last quarter's number are actually answering the same question about what 'active' requires.
A metric's growth is only meaningful if the bar for qualifying stayed the same. What would you need to do to make the two quarters genuinely comparable?

title: MasterClass's auto-play — completion up, cancellations naming the reason why
scenario_context: MasterClass tests auto-playing the next lesson in a course five seconds after the current one ends, replacing a screen that required a manual 'Next Lesson' click. Course completion rate rises 21%. But subscription cancellation rate, measured within 30 days of a completed course, rises from 6% to 11%, and cancellation survey responses increasingly cite 'felt like I was being pushed through content' as a reason.
description: What's the most defensible call?
options: Ship to 100% — a 21% completion-rate lift is a strong engagement signal, and a modest cancellation increase is a normal cost of a more engaging product.
Extend the test — 30 days isn't long enough to know whether the cancellation increase is a lasting pattern or a short-term artifact of the new flow.
Hold the rollout — the completion lift may be manufactured by removing a choice point rather than reflecting genuine interest, and the guardrail names the mechanism as the cause directly.
Ship, but only for courses under 6 lessons, since auto-play is more likely to feel forced across a longer course than a short one.
explanation: Option C is correct: completion rate rising because a screen that used to require an active choice to continue now continues by default isn't necessarily evidence people wanted to keep watching, it's at least partly evidence the path of least resistance changed, and the cancellation data is telling that same story directly rather than as background noise, subscribers are explicitly citing the exact mechanism, feeling pushed through content, as their reason for leaving. When the guardrail's own qualitative signal names the mechanism behind the primary metric's rise as the reason for churn, that's a stronger, more specific warning than a typical guardrail regression, and it should be resolved before rolling out further, not shipped past. Option A treats the cancellation increase as an expected, minor cost, but the survey responses aren't ambiguous background noise, they specifically implicate the change being tested as the reason subscribers are leaving, a much more direct signal than a generic trade-off. Option B's request for more time doesn't address what's already specific and interpretable in the data, the survey text is already explaining the mechanism, waiting longer doesn't change what subscribers are already saying about why they're canceling. Option D's course-length scoping is a plausible-sounding guess with no evidence behind it in the scenario, nothing given here breaks out the cancellation increase by course length, so this fix targets a hypothesis that hasn't actually been tested.
hints: Ask whether the completion metric moving is proof people wanted to keep watching, or whether it could just as easily reflect that continuing became the default rather than a choice.
The guardrail here isn't just a number — the qualitative reason attached to it may be telling you directly what's causing the primary metric to move. Weigh that connection.

title: Depop's response-rate ranking — does a length minimum stop the bots?
scenario_context: Depop ranks sellers partly by message response rate, the share of buyer messages a seller replies to within 24 hours, intended to reward responsive, trustworthy sellers. An analyst notices a cluster of sellers using third-party auto-reply bots that instantly send a generic 'Thanks, I'll get back to you soon!' to every message, counting as a reply for ranking purposes even when the seller never actually follows up with real information. A PM proposes: 'Fix this by requiring replies to be at least 20 characters long, since a real, thoughtful reply is longer than a one-line bot message.'
description: What's the flaw in the PM's proposed fix?
options: There's no flaw — a character-count minimum filters out the exact one-line message the bots are currently sending, closing the gaming hole.
A bot can trivially send a longer canned message that clears any character threshold, since the length requirement doesn't verify the reply is genuinely responsive.
The flaw is unrelated to gaming; a character minimum will simply frustrate sellers who prefer to communicate briefly and accurately.
The fix should instead remove response rate from the ranking entirely, since any behavioral metric based on messaging can eventually be automated.
explanation: Option B is correct: the fix targets the specific length of the current bot message, not the underlying capability being exploited, which is that a bot can send any text automatically regardless of content. A bot operator who wants to keep gaming the metric simply reconfigures the canned message to be longer, 'Thanks for reaching out! I'll review your question and get back to you with details as soon as I can' clears a 20-character bar easily while still being just as automated and just as devoid of real information as the original one-liner. The fix raises the cost of gaming by roughly nothing, changing a bot's template string is trivial. Option A assumes the current bot message's length is a fixed, meaningful signal rather than an arbitrary detail of how sellers happened to configure it today, but nothing about a longer automated message requires any more genuine responsiveness than a shorter one. Option C raises a real UX trade-off, but it doesn't identify why the fix fails at its stated goal, closing the gaming hole, it's a cost of the fix, not the flaw in its logic. Option D reaches for a more drastic response, dropping the metric, without first establishing that a better-designed version, checking for genuinely new information in a reply, say, couldn't work, abandoning the whole signal is a bigger move than the specific, fixable flaw in this fix calls for.
hints: Ask what a bot operator would actually have to change about their setup to get past this specific new rule, and whether that change requires anything genuinely different.
A fix that filters on a surface property of a message, like its length, doesn't close a gaming hole if that surface property is trivial for an automated system to fake.

title: Compass's close-rate matching — a faster deal, a harder landing for first-time buyers
scenario_context: Compass changes its buyer-agent matching algorithm to prioritize agents with the highest historical close-rate, reasoning that pairing buyers with agents who reliably get deals done should improve outcomes broadly. Deal close-rate for matched buyers rises 9%. But among first-time homebuyers specifically, a segment agents describe as needing more hand-holding, post-close satisfaction survey scores fall 15 points, and the same first-time-buyer segment shows a higher rate of deals falling through during financing, closer to the point of sale, than before the change.
description: What's the most defensible way to frame this result?
options: This is a clear win — a 9% close-rate lift is a strong commission-efficiency signal, and satisfaction surveys are a soft, secondary metric.
This is a clear loss — first-time buyers are a large, important segment, so the matching change should revert entirely regardless of the aggregate lift.
Name the trade-off by segment — high-close-rate agents may be optimizing for speed in a way that underserves first-time buyers, and the aggregate gain may be masking a real problem there.
Reframe entirely around total commission revenue, since that's the metric that most directly reflects whether the matching change is working for the business.
explanation: Option C is correct: the aggregate close-rate lift and the first-time-buyer-specific problems aren't necessarily in tension at the platform level, they may be two sides of the same mechanism, agents who close deals fastest may do so partly by moving buyers through quickly, which plausibly serves an experienced repeat buyer well but underserves a first-time buyer who needs more explanation and support, and the financing fall-through and satisfaction data are both concentrated in exactly that segment. Naming that segment-specific mechanism, rather than treating the aggregate number as the full story, is what the data actually supports. Option A treats the satisfaction drop as a soft, secondary signal to discount, but a financing fall-through is not soft, it's a deal that didn't close, in the exact segment the survey also flags, that's a hard outcome pointing the same direction as the qualitative concern. Option B jumps to a full reversion based on one segment's problems, discarding whatever real close-rate improvement is happening for buyers the new matching does serve well, without first checking whether a segment-aware matching rule, rather than an all-or-nothing revert, could address the first-time-buyer problem specifically. Option D swaps to a revenue metric not evidenced in the scenario at all, and sidesteps the actual, segment-specific pattern already visible in the data instead of engaging with it.
hints: The aggregate number and the segment-specific problems may not be two separate stories — ask whether the same agent behavior could explain both.
A fall-through during financing is a harder outcome than a survey score. Check which segment it's concentrated in before deciding how much weight the aggregate close-rate gain deserves.

title: Pokemon GO's referral loop — a Community Day spike versus the steady-state rate
scenario_context: Pokemon GO launches a referral feature: inviting a friend who reaches level 5 grants both players an exclusive item. During the feature's first week, which coincides with a globally-promoted in-game Community Day event, signups from referral links spike sharply, average invites sent per existing player briefly exceeds 1.3. Three weeks after Community Day ends, referral-driven signups fall to a steady rate of about 0.2 invites-that-convert per existing player per week.
description: What's the most defensible read of the referral loop's growth potential?
options: The loop is clearly viral and self-sustaining — the first week's k-factor above 1.3 proves that invited users are inviting more users in a compounding cycle.
The loop has failed and should be shut down — a drop from 1.3 to 0.2 invites-that-convert per player represents a near-total collapse in referral value.
The Community Day spike and the steady-state rate are the same underlying signal, just measured at different volumes, so the loop's true strength is best estimated by averaging the two.
The first week reflects burst virality tied to a promoted event, not the loop's sustained rate; 0.2 is the more representative number for judging whether the loop compounds on its own.
explanation: Option D is correct: a k-factor spiking during a globally-promoted event is exactly the shape of burst virality, a temporary surge driven by an external promotional push, not evidence of a self-sustaining loop, the number that actually answers whether this referral mechanic compounds on its own is the rate once the promotional tailwind is gone. At 0.2 converting invites per existing player per week, well under the k=1 threshold where a loop would be self-sustaining, the honest read is that this feature drives a real but modest, promotion-dependent boost rather than a compounding growth engine, and judging it by its steady-state number, not its event-week peak, is what determines whether it's a durable channel. Option A cites the event-week number as proof of a compounding cycle, but a k-factor measured during a period with an unusual external promotional driver doesn't isolate whether the mechanic itself, independent of that promotion, would sustain a cycle, the two are confounded. Option B treats the entire feature as a failure using the peak number as the baseline for comparison, but the peak was never a realistic steady-state expectation to hold the feature to, judging it against an inflated, event-driven number misreads what actually failed. Option C's averaging approach treats two structurally different measurements, one confounded by an external promotional event, one not, as interchangeable samples of the same thing, when they're actually answering different questions about the loop's behavior under different conditions.
hints: One of these two numbers was measured during an unusual promotional event, and one wasn't. Ask which one actually isolates the loop's own behavior.
A referral loop compounds on its own only above a specific threshold. Check which of the two numbers should be compared to that threshold to judge sustainability.

title: Angi's lead-volume drop — the seasonal verdict, and the bug found two weeks later
scenario_context: Angi's daily lead volume, homeowner requests submitted to contractors, fell 18% over 10 days. An analyst reports: 'This is just seasonal, home-service requests always dip this time of year, no action needed,' and closes the review. Two weeks later, engineering discovers a form-validation change shipped the same week the drop began, which silently rejected submissions where a homeowner's phone number included a country code prefix, common among a growing share of Angi's users.
description: What was the flaw in the analyst's original conclusion, given what engineering later found?
options: There was no flaw at the time; the analyst couldn't have known about a bug engineering hadn't yet found, so the seasonal explanation was reasonable given the information available.

The analyst treated a plausible seasonal story as sufficient without checking for a coincident technical change, exactly the kind of internally-verifiable cause a structured investigation checks before accepting an environmental explanation.
The flaw is that seasonal comparisons should always use a 4-week trailing average instead of a 10-day window, which would have revealed the bug faster.
The analyst should have escalated to engineering immediately regardless of the cause, since any metric drop warrants an engineering review as a first step.
explanation: Option B is correct: a seasonal explanation is a real, valid category of cause, but it's also the kind of story that's easy to accept without checking, and a disciplined investigation looks for recent, internally-verifiable changes, a deploy, a form update, a schema change, before settling on an environmental cause that's harder to falsify. The form-validation change shipped in the exact same window the drop began, and checking recent deploys against the metric's timeline is a fast, standard step that would have surfaced it, or at least flagged it as a hypothesis worth testing, well before engineering stumbled onto it two weeks later. Option A is sympathetic to the analyst but sidesteps the actual investigative gap, the point isn't that the analyst should have magically known about a bug nobody had found yet, it's that checking recent deploys against the timeline is a standard, doable step that wasn't taken, regardless of what it would have found. Option C proposes a specific technical fix to the comparison window that has nothing to do with the actual gap, a longer trailing average doesn't surface a form-validation bug any better than a 10-day window does. Option D overcorrects into a blanket rule, not every metric drop needs an engineering escalation as a first step, but checking the deploy log against the timeline, a much lighter first move, would have been the right early step here.
hints: A seasonal story is a real category of cause, but it's also the easiest one to accept without checking anything. What's a fast, standard check that should happen before settling on it?
The bug shipped in the exact same window the metric moved. What's the habit of checking recent changes against a metric's timeline meant to catch?

title: WeWork's overbooked hot desks — the airline analogy's limit
scenario_context: WeWork tests overbooking hot-desk memberships in high-demand locations, selling desk capacity at 115% of physical seats based on the historical no-show rate, similar to airline seat overbooking. Reported occupancy utilization and revenue-per-desk both rise meaningfully. In about 6% of measured days at overbooked locations, actual attendance exceeds physical capacity, and member complaints about 'couldn't find a place to work' rise sharply on exactly those days.
description: What's the most defensible strategic call?
options: Keep the overbooking rate as-is — the revenue and utilization gains are real and substantial, and complaints occur on a small minority of days.
Increase the overbooking rate further, since the current 115% level is clearly tolerable and a higher rate would capture even more revenue upside.
Revert to no overbooking at any location, since a coworking membership's core promise is guaranteed workspace access, and any risk of that failing is unacceptable.

Lower the overbooking rate specifically at locations with the highest no-show variability, since a member unable to find a desk is a direct breach of what a membership promises, in a way a full flight isn't for most travelers.
explanation: Option D is correct: the airline analogy the overbooking strategy borrows from actually breaks down on the exact point that matters here, a bumped airline passenger gets rebooked and compensated within a system built to absorb that outcome, but a member who shows up to a workspace and can't find a desk has nowhere else to go in that moment, their workday is just disrupted, which makes a coworking membership's capacity promise a harder line than a flight's. The fix that respects this is scoping the overbooking rate down specifically where no-show behavior is least predictable, the locations generating the capacity breaches, rather than treating the strategy as uniformly safe or uniformly unacceptable. Option A treats a 6%-of-days failure rate as an acceptable minority cost, but that framing undercounts what member trust in a workspace membership actually depends on, a member who hits full capacity even occasionally may stop trusting the membership at all. Option B extends a strategy already producing real capacity breaches without addressing why they're happening, chasing more revenue upside from the same mechanism that's already causing member-facing failures. Option C swings to eliminating overbooking everywhere, discarding a real revenue and utilization gain at the many locations where no-show rates are stable and predictable enough that capacity was never actually breached, a broader response than the uneven, location-specific failure pattern supports.
hints: The airline-overbooking analogy has a limit. Ask what actually happens to a bumped airline passenger, and whether a member who can't find a desk has anything comparable available to them.
The capacity breaches aren't happening everywhere equally. Check what's different about the locations where they occur before deciding whether the whole strategy needs to change.

title: Rippling's expense-management sizing — a $45M ceiling, not a forecast
scenario_context: Rippling is sizing a new expense-management add-on for its existing HR/IT platform customers. An analyst's estimate: Rippling has 20,000 business customers; industry data says the average company spends $50/employee/year on expense-management software; Rippling's customers average 45 employees; therefore the total addressable spend is 20,000 x 45 x $50 = $45M/year, presented to leadership as the opportunity size for this add-on.
description: What's the strongest reason to be skeptical of treating the full $45M as the add-on's realistic opportunity?
options: The estimate assumes every customer would switch its entire expense-management spend to Rippling's add-on, but converting existing customers from an installed competitor typically captures only a fraction of that population, not all of it.
The $50/employee/year industry average is likely outdated and should be re-sourced from a more recent industry report before the estimate is trusted.
The estimate should be adjusted for Rippling's historical customer churn rate, since some of the 20,000 customers will churn before the add-on even launches.
45 employees is an average, not a median, so the estimate should be recomputed using the median company size to avoid distortion from a few very large customers.
explanation: Option A is correct: the calculation sizes the total expense-management spend across Rippling's entire customer base as if the add-on would capture all of it, but most of those customers already have some expense-management solution in place, a spreadsheet, a competitor's tool, an internal process, and converting an existing customer away from whatever they currently use, to a brand-new, unproven add-on from their HR platform, realistically captures some meaningful fraction of that population and their spend, not the entire base at full value. The $45M figure is better read as a ceiling that bounds the true opportunity from above, not as the opportunity itself. Option B raises a fair data-freshness question, but even a perfectly current, well-sourced industry average wouldn't fix the deeper issue, the estimate still assumes total conversion of every customer's existing spend, which is the larger source of overstatement here. Option C's churn adjustment is a real, generally reasonable correction, but it's a comparatively minor one next to the core problem, assuming 100% of the customer base adopts and fully switches spend is a much bigger overstatement than losing a modest share to churn before launch. Option D's mean-versus-median point is a legitimate general estimation habit, but nothing in the scenario suggests Rippling's customer-size distribution is skewed enough to meaningfully distort this specific number, and it doesn't address the much larger conversion-rate assumption baked into the calculation.
hints: Ask where the money for this add-on's revenue is actually supposed to come from — is it money customers aren't already spending elsewhere, or spend that has to be won away from something else?

A top-down calculation that multiplies a whole population by a spend average is answering 'how big is the total pie,' not 'how much of it would actually convert.' What's missing between those two numbers?

title: Waymo's downtown expansion — strong demand, one intersection cluster
scenario_context: Waymo is deciding whether to expand robotaxi service from its current geofenced zone into a new, denser downtown district. A 6-week pilot with a small supervised fleet in the new district shows strong ride demand, projected utilization well above the current zone's average. But the pilot also logs a higher rate of 'unexpected maneuver' safety interventions per mile, mostly at a specific cluster of complex, unprotected-left-turn intersections, than Waymo's current zone has ever recorded.
description: What's the most defensible call?
options: Expand to the full new district immediately — strong ride demand is the clearest signal that this market is ready, and safety systems exist precisely to catch these interventions before harm occurs.
Expand, but only during daytime hours, since visibility-related factors are the most common cause of autonomous-vehicle safety interventions generally.
Do not expand at all, and do not retest — a rise in intervention rate at any location is disqualifying for a physical-safety-critical product, regardless of magnitude or cause.
Expand to the new district except the specific intersection cluster driving the elevated rate, while engineering addresses that maneuver type, and revisit the excluded area once resolved.
explanation: Option D is correct: the elevated intervention rate isn't spread evenly across the new district, it's concentrated at an identifiable, specific class of intersection, unprotected left turns, in one cluster, which means the risk is scoped and addressable rather than a general sign the whole district is unsafe for the current system. Launching everywhere except the specific geography driving the signal captures the real, strong demand across the rest of the district while withholding service exactly where the safety system is already telling the team it needs more work, and revisiting that area once the maneuver is addressed is a defensible, evidence-based path back to full coverage. Option A treats demand as the deciding factor and treats the safety system catching interventions as proof the risk is already handled, but a rising intervention rate at a specific, identifiable location is a signal to investigate and address, not evidence the system has already solved the problem, that's precisely backwards from how a safety-critical product should read its own guardrail. Option B guesses at a specific mechanism, visibility, not evidenced anywhere in the scenario, the intervention cluster is described as being about a maneuver type, unprotected left turns, not about lighting or time of day, so a daytime-only restriction doesn't address the actual pattern found. Option C treats any intervention-rate increase anywhere as fully disqualifying regardless of how scoped or addressable it is, and refuses even a future retest, a response more drastic than a specific, geographically-isolated, engineering-addressable finding calls for.
hints: The elevated rate isn't happening everywhere in the new district — check what's specific about where it's concentrated before deciding whether the whole expansion is the thing in question.

A safety guardrail catching more interventions in one specific spot is a signal to investigate that spot, not proof the system has already absorbed the risk. What's the difference between those two readings?

title: PayPal's default Pay-in-4 — checkout completion up, plan-stacking defaults rising
scenario_context: PayPal tests showing its 'Pay in 4' installment option more prominently at checkout, defaulting it as the pre-selected payment method for eligible purchases instead of requiring an extra tap to find it. Two-week result: checkout completion rises 8%, the stated primary metric. The guardrail, 90-day default rate on Pay-in-4 plans, rises from 3% to 7%, and the increase is concentrated almost entirely among users who now hold 3 or more concurrent Pay-in-4 plans at once, a pattern uncommon before this test.
description: What's the most defensible call?
options: Ship to 100% — an 8% checkout-completion lift is a strong primary-metric result, and a 4-point default-rate rise is a modest cost for a payments feature.
Hold the rollout — the default-rate increase is concentrated in users stacking multiple concurrent plans, a cost to both users and PayPal's credit exposure.
Ship, but only measure success by checkout completion going forward, since that's the metric the placement change directly targeted.
Extend the test — a 90-day default window means the results aren't even fully observed yet for the most recent cohorts in the test.
explanation: Option B is correct: the guardrail isn't just moving, it's moving in a way that traces to a specific, plausible mechanism — making Pay-in-4 the default, easier-to-reach option increases how often it gets chosen without a deliberate decision, and a share of users are stacking several concurrent plans as a result, a pattern that raises real default risk for those users and real credit exposure for PayPal. This is a case where the checkout lift and the guardrail regression may be two faces of the same behavior, more defaulting-in to a credit product without fully weighing whether taking on another one is wise, so shipping broadly risks locking in a costly pattern before understanding it. Option A treats the default-rate increase as a generic, minor cost without engaging with the specific mechanism, plan-stacking, that the concentration points to, a guardrail this specifically traceable to the change itself isn't background noise. Option C commits to tracking only the metric the change was built to move, exactly the blind spot that lets a real cost go unmonitored once the guardrail stops being checked. Option D's timing objection has some truth to it, but the concentration in stacked-plan users is already a strong, interpretable signal on its own, without needing every last cohort's 90-day window to close before it's worth acting on.
hints: The guardrail's increase isn't spread evenly — it's concentrated in a specific behavioral pattern. Ask what the placement change might be encouraging that pattern to happen.
Two things may be connected here rather than separate: what made checkout easier, and what's driving up default risk. Check whether they share a mechanism.

title: Merchant partnerships push back — 'this is unambiguous upside, don't slow it down'
scenario_context: PayPal's merchant partnerships team pushes back on any rollback of the Pay-in-4 default placement: merchants pay PayPal a per-transaction fee and have seen real checkout-completion gains, and the partnerships lead argues 'this is unambiguously good for merchants, don't let a credit-risk concern that's internal to PayPal's own balance sheet slow down a feature merchants are asking to keep.' The credit-risk team maintains its position that plan-stacking is a real, growing exposure.
description: What's the most defensible way to frame this disagreement?
options: Defer entirely to the merchant partnerships team — they represent the revenue-generating side of the business, and completion gains are concrete and already realized.
Defer entirely to the credit-risk team — default risk is a financial liability, and any pushback from a revenue-facing team should be treated as a conflict of interest.
Name the trade-off — merchant gains are real, but partly funded by user over-extension; a scoped fix, like capping concurrent plans, may serve both sides better.
Ask the merchant partnerships team to survey merchants directly on whether they'd accept a stricter Pay-in-4 eligibility rule, and let that survey decide the outcome.
explanation: Option C is correct: the partnerships lead's framing treats this as merchant upside with no downside, but the default rate is rising because of the same placement change driving the completion gain, the two aren't separable, one team's win is partly funded by the exposure the other team is flagging. Rather than treating this as a contest between two teams' priorities, a cap on concurrent Pay-in-4 plans targets the exact mechanism, stacking, driving the default-rate increase without necessarily removing the more prominent placement that's helping merchant completion broadly, which is a design response to the actual trade-off rather than a verdict on which internal team should win. Option A accepts the partnerships team's one-sided framing and defers to the loudest, most immediate voice, ignoring that the credit exposure is a real cost with its own claim on the decision, not a lesser, purely internal concern. Option B swings to the opposite one-sided deferral, dismissing merchant completion gains as unimportant and treating the revenue-facing team's input as inherently suspect, when their observation about merchant value is also factually accurate. Option D outsources the decision to a survey of merchants, who aren't positioned to weigh PayPal's own credit-risk exposure, a question about PayPal's balance-sheet risk isn't one merchants have the visibility or incentive to answer well.
hints: One team is describing a real gain and the other a real cost, and they may both be right at the same time — check whether the two are actually connected rather than being an either-or.
A stakeholder pushing hard for their side's number doesn't mean the other side's concern is invalid. Look for a response that addresses the actual mechanism both sides are reacting to.

title: Generalizing beyond this one feature — the principle for any future credit product
scenario_context: Stepping back from the Pay-in-4 placement decision specifically, PayPal's leadership asks the team to propose a general principle for how any future BNPL or credit-adjacent feature should be evaluated before launch, not just this one case.
description: Which principle best generalizes the lesson from the Pay-in-4 result to PayPal's credit products as a strategic class?
options: Any feature that increases short-term completion or revenue should launch by default, and credit-risk review should only apply after a feature has already shown a problem in production.
Any credit feature that can change how much total obligation a user takes on, not just whether one transaction completes, needs a concurrent-exposure guardrail defined before launch.
PayPal should stop testing default-placement changes for any credit product entirely, since this result shows defaults are inherently manipulative for financial features.
Every future credit-adjacent feature should be tested only on existing Pay-in-4 users, since that population's behavior is already understood from this test.
explanation: Option B is correct: the generalizable lesson from Pay-in-4 isn't about this one placement choice, it's that a credit product's real risk lives in a dimension a single-transaction completion metric doesn't see at all, how much total obligation a user is accumulating across products, and that dimension needs to be instrumented and gated before launch, not discovered after default rates already climbed. That's the class of feature, and the class of guardrail, this result actually points to as a durable rule. Option A takes the opposite lesson from what happened, this specific case is a direct demonstration of why waiting for a production problem to trigger risk review is exactly the failure mode that let plan-stacking grow unnoticed until the guardrail caught it. Option C overgeneralizes from one result to a blanket rule against an entire design pattern, default placement, when the actual fix that emerged, a concurrent-exposure guardrail, addresses the underlying risk without requiring PayPal to abandon default-placement design for every credit feature going forward. Option D narrows future testing to a population already exposed to this specific product, which doesn't generalize the lesson to new credit-adjacent features at all, a genuinely new feature would have its own new population and its own new exposure dynamics to instrument for, not just this one's existing users.
hints: The lesson isn't really about default placement specifically. Ask what dimension of risk this result revealed that a single-transaction metric structurally can't see.
A durable principle should apply to a feature PayPal hasn't built yet. Which option describes a rule for a whole class of future features, not just a fix for this one?

title: Glassdoor's Employer Trust Score — designing against a coordinated review burst
scenario_context: Glassdoor is designing an 'Employer Trust Score' shown prominently on company profile pages, and wants it resistant to a known gaming pattern: some HR teams organize internal campaigns urging employees to post positive reviews all at once, right before a scheduled score recalculation, temporarily inflating the average rating with a burst of solicited, less-candid reviews.
description: Which candidate scoring design is most resistant to this kind of coordinated, solicited review burst?
options: Score based on average rating alone, recalculated weekly, so any coordinated burst is quickly incorporated and reflected transparently.
Score based on average rating from reviews spread across a rolling 12-month window, weighted so no single week can contribute more than a small, capped share of the total.
Score based on total review count alone, since a company that solicits more reviews is at least generating more employee engagement with the platform.
Score based on average rating, but exclude reviews submitted during any week where review volume spikes more than 3x the company's typical weekly rate.
explanation: Option B is correct: capping how much any single week can contribute to a rolling average directly neutralizes the exact mechanic being exploited, a coordinated burst timed right before a recalculation. Even if HR successfully organizes a large wave of reviews in one week, that wave's weight in the score is bounded, so its influence on the trust score is limited regardless of how big the burst gets, while genuine, steadily-arriving reviews across the year continue to carry their normal weight. Option A's weekly recalculation on a simple average does the opposite of resisting the gaming pattern, a well-timed burst has maximum, undiluted influence on a metric recalculated right after it lands, which is precisely the vulnerability described. Option C rewards review volume directly, which is exactly what a solicitation campaign is designed to produce, more reviews, regardless of whether they're candid or coordinated, so it doesn't resist the gaming pattern, it directly rewards it. Option D's spike-detection threshold sounds targeted, but a coordinated campaign can be timed and paced to stay under a 3x threshold, spreading solicited reviews across two or three weeks instead of one, defeating a single-week volume trigger while still achieving the same inflated result.
hints: Ask what a coordinated review campaign is actually capable of controlling, timing and volume, and whether each design still lets that control translate into an outsized score effect.
A score resists a timed burst when no single short window, however large, can dominate the number on its own.

title: Generalizing the vulnerability beyond Glassdoor, and beyond employer reviews
scenario_context: Having designed a burst-resistant version of the Employer Trust Score, Glassdoor's leadership asks the team to generalize the finding: across any platform that publishes a trust or reputation score built from user-submitted signals, not just Glassdoor, what class of design is inherently vulnerable to the same coordinated-burst attack?
description: Which generalization correctly identifies the vulnerable class?
options: Any score built from a time-unweighted aggregate of user-submitted signals is vulnerable, since a large, well-timed burst can dominate a total that treats every contribution equally.
Only scores specifically about employer reputation are vulnerable, since employees are the only population with enough shared incentive to coordinate a submission burst.
Any score that updates in real time is inherently ungameable, since real-time updates make coordinated timing pointless.
The vulnerability is specific to review-based platforms; scores built from behavioral data, like purchase history, don't share this risk.
explanation: Option A is correct: the actual mechanism exposed by the Glassdoor case is structural, not employer-specific, any reputation score that aggregates submitted signals without bounding how much a short, concentrated window can contribute treats a coordinated burst the same as organic, spread-out contributions, and organic contributions have no coordination advantage while a motivated party's burst does. That structural gap, not anything unique to employee reviews, is what makes a design vulnerable, and it would apply identically to product reviews, ratings platforms, or any other submitted-signal reputation system built the same way. Option B narrows the vulnerability to employer reputation specifically, but nothing about the mechanism, a large coordinated submission wave dominating an unweighted aggregate, is unique to employees, any population with a shared incentive to coordinate, sellers on a marketplace, app developers, could exploit the identical structural gap. Option C gets the direction backwards, real-time updating is what makes a burst's timing most effective, not least, since the burst gets reflected in the score before it can be diluted by the normal, steady flow of unrelated future signals. Option D assumes behavioral data is immune, but coordinated behavior, a group deliberately manufacturing a batch of purchases or actions at a chosen moment, can dominate a behavioral aggregate through the same unweighted-time-window gap, the underlying vulnerability is about how the aggregate treats time and volume, not about what kind of signal is being aggregated.
hints: Ask what specifically made the Glassdoor coordinated-burst exploit work, and whether that mechanism depends on anything unique to employee reviews specifically.
The vulnerability lives in how an aggregate treats timing and volume, not in what kind of signal, review, rating, behavior, is being aggregated. Which option names that general structural property?

title: Sales objects — new customers can't move the score fast enough anymore
scenario_context: Glassdoor's sales team objects to the burst-resistant design: they routinely encourage newly-onboarded employer customers to run a legitimate, above-board campaign asking real employees for honest reviews in their first month, and the capped rolling-window design means even a genuine, well-intentioned early push from a new customer won't move their score quickly, which the sales team says makes the product a harder sell to onboard.
description: What's the most defensible response to the sales team's concern?
options: Remove the rolling-window cap for the first 90 days of any new employer's account, since new customers haven't had time to accumulate an organic review history yet.
Reject the sales team's concern entirely — a review score that moves quickly for anyone is definitionally gameable, and no exception should exist.
Keep the general design uncapped-for-everyone, since a slower-moving score for new customers is an acceptable cost of closing the coordinated-burst hole for the whole platform.
Give sales team members visibility into projected score movement so they can set new-customer expectations accurately, without changing the underlying scoring mechanics themselves.
explanation: Option D is correct: the sales team's actual problem is an expectations and communication gap, not a flaw in the scoring design itself, a new customer's genuine early review push still counts and still moves the score, it just moves it at the same bounded rate the design intentionally applies to everyone, and giving sales a clear, honest way to set that expectation solves their onboarding-pitch problem without reopening the exact vulnerability the redesign closed. Option A creates a new-customer exception that recreates precisely the hole just fixed, a coordinated burst timed within a new account's first 90 days would be just as effective as the original gaming pattern, an adversarial party only needs to time their account's life stage to exploit it. Option B dismisses a real, legitimate business concern, sales does have an actual onboarding friction point worth addressing, without offering any path to address it, treating every accommodation as automatically illegitimate isn't itself a principled distinction from the coordinated-burst case. Option C accepts the trade-off exists but proposes no actual resolution for the sales team's stated problem, leaving the friction unaddressed when a lower-cost fix, better expectation-setting, is available.
hints: Ask whether the sales team's actual problem is that the scoring design is wrong, or that nobody's told them clearly how it behaves for a new customer.
A fix that reopens the exact vulnerability the redesign was built to close isn't a real fix — check whether any proposed accommodation could be exploited the same way as the original gaming pattern.

title: Behance's Discover feed rebuild — engagement is up, exposure is collapsing onto a shrinking pool of creators
scenario_context: Adobe's Behance rebuilds its Discover feed ranking to optimize directly for session dwell time and Appreciates (its like mechanic) instead of recency. Post-launch, aggregate dwell time per session is up 14% and Appreciates per session are up 9%, but a portfolio-level breakdown shows the top 1% most-followed creators now capture 58% of all Discover impressions, up from 35% before the change, while creators who joined in the past six months see Discover-driven profile views fall by more than 80%, even for portfolios matching the historical quality bar for featured work. Leadership, pointing to the aggregate engagement numbers, wants to call the redesign a clear win and ship to 100%.
description: At the strategic, portfolio level, what's the most defensible way to evaluate whether this redesign is actually a win?
options: Revert Discover to a strictly chronological feed with no engagement-based ranking at all, since any signal built from follows or past Appreciates will eventually reproduce this same concentration.
Reframe success around the number of distinct creators who receive at least one Appreciate that week, since a wider spread of appreciation reflects a healthier community than raw dwell time alone.
Ship as planned — a ranking model that surfaces already-popular work more often is simply reflecting quality signal accumulated through follows and past Appreciates, not a flaw to second-guess.
Pair the engagement gain with a guardrail on emerging-creator reach — aggregate dwell time and Appreciates rising isn't success on its own if new work is getting harder to find on merit.
explanation: Option D is correct: the aggregate numbers describe what happened to the average session, not to the platform's supply side, and Behance's actual differentiator, the reason a creator posts here instead of just building a following on a general social feed, is the promise that quality work can still get discovered on its own merit. A redesign that lifts dwell time and Appreciates while collapsing exposure for quality-matched new creators by more than 80% is trading away exactly that promise, so declaring the launch a win on the aggregate numbers alone treats a structural supply-side cost as if it doesn't exist. The defensible read pairs the engagement gain with an explicit guardrail on emerging-creator reach before calling this a strategic success, not after the concentration has already hollowed out the pipeline of new creators the platform depends on long-term. Option A swings to the opposite extreme: removing engagement-based ranking entirely would also remove the one thing that makes Discover useful as a discovery tool in the first place, a purely chronological feed drowns quality-matched new work in the full, undifferentiated volume of everything else newly posted, which doesn't actually help the emerging creators it's meant to protect. Option B sounds like it addresses the equity concern but sets a bar so low, one single Appreciate in a week, that it could be satisfied by a stray, incidental like while a creator's real Discover exposure stays collapsed; it doesn't measure or gate the actual concentration mechanism the scenario describes. Option C takes the model's own output as self-justifying, but the scenario already rules out the 'it's just quality winning' explanation: creators posting work that matches the historical bar for featured placement are still nearly disappearing from Discover, which means the concentration is coming from an accumulated-following advantage the ranking amplifies, not from a fresh read of each post's quality.
hints: Two different things moved here: what happened to the average session, and what happened to the distribution of exposure across creators. Check whether the first can look great while the second quietly breaks something the platform depends on.

One option treats 'popularity concentrated because of the ranking' and 'popularity concentrated because of quality' as the same explanation. The scenario already gives you evidence to tell those two apart, look for it.

title: Define 'findable on merit' — leadership isn't giving you one
scenario_context: The team adopts the paired-guardrail approach, but leadership pushes back in the design review: 'You keep saying new work should stay findable on merit. Define exactly what that means as something we can track. I'm not giving you a definition, that's your job to propose and defend.'
description: Which proposed operational definition of 'findable on merit' best translates the strategic goal into something the team can actually measure?
options: Median Discover impressions per quality-score unit for new creators, controlling for the poster's existing follower count.
Average number of Appreciates a new creator's most recent project receives within its first 24 hours after posting.
Total Discover impressions delivered to every account created in the past six months, summed across the entire cohort.
Number of new creators who land a recruiter or brand inquiry through their Behance profile within their first month of joining.
explanation: Option A is correct: 'findable on merit' only means something measurable if the definition explicitly separates the two things currently tangled together, how good a project is and how many followers its creator already has, and this is the only option built to do that. Normalizing a new creator's impressions by an independent quality score while controlling for follower count directly tests whether a quality-matched newcomer is actually getting seen, which is exactly the question the redesign's own data left open. It's also something the team can log today: an independent quality score, a curator or peer-review rating, already exists or is buildable, follower count is already tracked, and Discover impressions are already logged per project. Option B measures Appreciates, but Appreciates are themselves downstream of exposure, and exposure is downstream of follower count under the current ranking, so a creator who already has an established following will out-score a quality-matched newcomer on this metric for the same reason they out-score them on raw impressions, it inherits the exact contamination the definition is supposed to isolate. Option C sums impressions across an entire cohort of new accounts, which rises automatically as more people sign up and post more, whether or not any individual quality-matched newcomer's odds of being seen have improved at all, a metric that moves with signup volume isn't measuring findability. Option D points at a real, desirable outcome, but a recruiter or brand inquiry is rare, slow to arrive, and shaped by hiring demand and channels far outside Discover's ranking, too lagging and confounded to function as a trackable operational metric for a specific feed redesign.
hints: The term needs to separate two things that are currently tangled together in the data you already have, how good a piece of work is, and how many followers its creator already has. Which candidate actually isolates one from the other?

A good operational definition should move independently of signup volume and independently of a creator's pre-existing following. Check which candidates would rise for reasons that have nothing to do with an individual project actually being found.

title: Partnerships team's top-creator exposure falls as designed — defend the trade-off
scenario_context: Behance's Creative Partnerships team, which manages brand-sponsorship deals built around the platform's most-followed creators, reports that Discover impressions for their top-tier partner creators have fallen roughly 15% since the reach guardrail shipped, exactly the reallocation the guardrail was designed to produce, and the partnerships lead is asking leadership to roll it back given the sponsorship revenue tied to those creators' visibility.
description: What's the most defensible way to frame this trade-off for leadership?
options: Roll back the guardrail — sponsorship revenue tied to top-tier creator visibility is Behance's most direct monetization lever, and a strategic guardrail shouldn't threaten it.
Name the trade-off directly — the reallocation was the guardrail's intended mechanism, and rising quality-normalized newcomer reach shows it's working as designed.
Reject the partnerships team's concern outright — once a strategic guardrail is adopted, revenue impact on any single stakeholder team shouldn't factor into the conversation at all.
Redefine success around top-tier partner-creator impressions going forward, since that's a more concrete, revenue-relevant number than an abstract reach guardrail.
explanation: Option B is correct: this isn't a surprising cost that appeared after the fact, it's the direct, mechanical result of the exact reallocation the guardrail was built to produce, so the conversation with the partnerships team should start by naming that this trade-off was already implicit in adopting the guardrail in the first place. The fact that quality-normalized reach for newcomers is rising is the evidence that matters here: it shows the guardrail is doing precisely what it was designed to do, and citing that alongside the partnerships team's number keeps the decision grounded in the trade-off leadership already chose, rather than re-litigating it every time one side of it becomes visible to a stakeholder. Option A treats the partnerships team's revenue concern as automatically decisive and rolls back a guardrail that was adopted deliberately, without weighing that the guardrail's entire purpose was to accept exactly this kind of reallocation. Option C swings to the opposite extreme, refusing to weigh a real, legitimate business concern at all once a guardrail exists, which isn't more rigorous than deferring to it, it's just as one-sided in the other direction. Option D proposes replacing the very signal the guardrail was designed to move, quality-normalized newcomer reach, with the number the reallocation was intentionally designed to reduce, which would quietly undo the strategic decision under stakeholder pressure rather than defend it.
hints: Ask whether the partnerships team's number falling is a surprising side effect, or something that was always the direct, mechanical consequence of the guardrail leadership already chose to adopt.

One metric falling while another rises might be exactly the evidence the trade-off is working as intended, not a sign that something has gone wrong. Which metric is that here, and what does its movement actually tell you?

title: Walmart's grocery pickup on-time rate drops during a holiday, a pilot app rolls out the same week
scenario_context: Walmart's grocery pickup on-time rate (orders ready within the promised window) fell from 93% to 86% over the past three weeks, during the week of a major holiday. Two candidate explanations are already on the table: last year showed a comparable seasonal dip during the same holiday week, 93% to 87%, consistent with higher order volume straining staffing. Separately, a subset of stores began piloting a new in-store picking app three weeks ago, and for privacy reasons tied to a new data-handling agreement with the app vendor, individual store-level pilot participation isn't visible in the standard company-wide dashboard the team is using.
description: Given a recurring seasonal pattern, a plausible new-tool cause, and a constraint on what the data can currently show, what's the most defensible first move?
options: Request store-level pilot-participation data through an approved channel, so the picking-app hypothesis can actually be tested against the seasonal one.
Accept the seasonal explanation as sufficient, since a comparable dip happened last year during the same holiday week, and move on without further investigation.
Recommend pausing the picking-app pilot immediately as a precaution, since a new tool coinciding with a metric drop is reason enough to halt it pending investigation.
Wait until next month's dashboard refresh, when the data-handling agreement's initial restriction period is expected to lift, before doing anything further.
explanation: Option A is correct: two real, plausible explanations are on the table, and the standard dashboard's current blind spot, not seeing which stores are piloting the new app, is exactly what's preventing the team from testing one of them, so the defensible move is getting that specific, narrowly-scoped data through a channel that still respects the agreement, rather than either accepting the untested seasonal story or guessing. Once pilot-store participation is visible, the team can directly compare pilot-store on-time rates against non-pilot stores' rates this same holiday week, which would cleanly separate a tool-driven effect from a seasonal one that should hit every store regardless of pilot status. Option B accepts a real, plausible pattern as sufficient without ruling out the second real, plausible cause sitting right alongside it, especially when a specific, checkable comparison, pilot versus non-pilot stores, is available if the data constraint is worked around properly. Option C jumps to an operational action, pausing the pilot, before confirming whether the pilot is actually connected to the drop at all, a bigger and more disruptive move than the evidence yet supports, and one that a proper comparison could avoid making unnecessarily. Option D treats the data constraint as fixed and waits passively for it to lift on its own timeline, when the more defensible path is actively requesting the specific data through an approved channel now, rather than letting an investigation stall on an assumed timeline.
hints: Two real explanations are on the table, and one of them can't currently be tested because of a specific data visibility gap. Ask whether that gap can be worked around properly rather than accepted as a dead end.
The comparison that would actually separate a seasonal cause from a tool-driven one is available if the right data becomes visible. What's the responsible way to get access to it?

title: The pilot effect traces to employees on the app for under two weeks
scenario_context: The requested pilot data comes back: on-time rate at pilot stores is only lower specifically on shifts staffed by employees with less than two weeks of tenure using the new picking app; pilot-store shifts staffed by employees with more tenure on the app show on-time rates matching non-pilot stores. Fewer than 15% of pilot-store shifts fall into this new-employee category.
description: Does this finding change the read on the picking-app hypothesis, and how?
options: No — the pilot app is still implicated in the drop regardless of which employees are using it, since the app was the change introduced at pilot stores.
No — a sub-population under 15% of shifts is too small to be meaningful, and the seasonal explanation should be treated as the primary cause instead.
Yes — this narrows the cause to a specific, small sub-population, new employees still learning the app, pointing toward a training gap, not a flaw in the tool.
Yes — this proves the app itself is fine, and the entire on-time rate drop, including at non-pilot stores, should now be attributed to the holiday season alone.
explanation: Option C is correct: the finding doesn't clear the app of involvement, it sharpens exactly what about the app rollout is responsible, tenured users of the same app perform identically to non-pilot stores, so the tool itself isn't structurally slower or worse, the drop is concentrated in a specific, small, identifiable transitional population still climbing the learning curve. That's a materially different, more actionable finding than 'the app caused a drop,' it points at a training or ramp-up gap to fix, not a reason to reconsider the tool's design. Option A treats the app as implicated in some undifferentiated way, ignoring that the data just showed a clean split, tenured-user shifts are unaffected, which is exactly the kind of segment-level finding that should update the read rather than being waved off as irrelevant. Option B dismisses a clean, mechanistically-sensible segment finding because the affected population's share is small, but a small population can still be the entire explanation for a metric movement when its own internal rate is meaningfully different, and here it explains the tool-related portion precisely. Option D draws a conclusion the finding doesn't support at all, showing that new-app-users specifically underperform says nothing about whether the holiday's seasonal effect on non-pilot stores was real or not, those are separate populations experiencing separate causes.
hints: The affected population is both small and specific. Ask what that combination, a clean split between new and tenured users of the same tool, actually tells you about where the problem lives.
A finding this precisely scoped, unaffected for one group, affected for a narrow, identifiable other group, usually points toward a specific fix rather than toward abandoning the broader conclusion.

title: A logging bug hits exactly the new-employee segment already flagged
scenario_context: The picking-app engineering team reports a separate finding: for the exact three-week window in question, a bug caused the app to mis-log shift-start times specifically for employees on their first two weeks of app access, some of their early shift time was recorded as starting later than it actually did, which would make their on-time performance look worse than it actually was, independent of any real training-related slowness.
description: Given this new information, what's the most defensible next step before concluding the training-gap explanation is correct?
options: Conclude the training-gap explanation was wrong all along, and that the entire new-employee effect is fully explained by the logging bug instead.
Since both a training gap and a logging bug are now plausible, average the two effects together to produce a single, blended corrected estimate.
Disregard the new-employee segment finding entirely now that a data quality issue has been found in it, and revert to treating the seasonal explanation as primary.
Recompute new-employee on-time performance using an independent timestamp source unaffected by the bug, to see how much of the gap remains once the logging error is corrected for.
explanation: Option D is correct: a confirmed logging bug affecting exactly the population already flagged as low-performing means that population's numbers can no longer be trusted at face value, but it doesn't mean the underlying training-gap explanation is wrong, it means the two explanations, real slowness and measurement error, need to be separated using a source the bug doesn't touch. Recomputing the affected shifts' actual performance from an independent timestamp source is the direct way to find out how much of the observed gap survives correction, which is the only way to know whether a real training issue remains once the bug's contribution is removed. Option A jumps to the opposite extreme, declaring the bug fully explains the effect with no verification that it does, exactly the kind of unearned confidence a single plausible new explanation shouldn't get without checking the corrected numbers. Option B's averaging approach treats two explanations of unknown relative size as if splitting the difference were itself a form of rigor, but nothing supports a 50/50 split specifically, the actual answer requires recomputing the real numbers, not blending unverified estimates. Option C discards a segment finding that's still real, new employees experiencing a logging bug doesn't mean new employees aren't also slower on a new tool, it discards a legitimate lead because part of its measurement turned out to be compromised, rather than fixing the measurement and checking what remains.
hints: A logging bug affecting the exact population already flagged doesn't mean that population's underlying story is now fully explained, it means the measurement needs to be redone with a source the bug doesn't touch.
Ask what would be left of the new-employee effect if the specific measurement error were corrected for, rather than assuming the bug either fully explains it or doesn't matter at all.

title: TaskRabbit's IKEA routing — faster arrival, lower ratings, unhappy top Taskers
scenario_context: TaskRabbit partners with IKEA to offer furniture-assembly Taskers bookable directly from IKEA's checkout flow. A change routes IKEA-sourced assembly bookings to whichever Tasker can arrive soonest, rather than the Tasker with the highest customer rating in the area. IKEA reports faster average booking-to-arrival time and higher attach-rate of assembly service at checkout. TaskRabbit's own marketplace data shows post-assembly customer ratings for IKEA-sourced jobs are meaningfully lower than for jobs booked directly through the TaskRabbit app, and top-rated Taskers report getting fewer IKEA-sourced jobs than before.
description: What's the most defensible way to frame this three-way result?
options: This is a clear win for the partnership — IKEA's attach-rate and arrival-speed metrics improved, and that's the commercial relationship TaskRabbit needs to protect.
This is a clear loss — customer ratings fell, so the fastest-arrival routing should revert to rating-based routing for all IKEA bookings immediately.
Name the three-way trade-off — IKEA's checkout metrics improved, but likely at the cost of job quality and top-rated Tasker satisfaction.
Reframe success around total IKEA-sourced booking volume, since that most directly reflects whether the partnership itself is working.
explanation: Option C is correct: three different parties are experiencing three different effects here, and they're plausibly connected rather than independent, routing for speed over rating systematically deprioritizes top-rated Taskers who may not be the fastest available, which would explain both the lower post-assembly ratings and those Taskers reporting fewer IKEA jobs, at the same time it's genuinely improving the checkout-facing metrics IKEA cares about. TaskRabbit's marketplace depends on both a happy commercial partner and a trustworthy pool of highly-rated Taskers willing to keep taking jobs, so naming the trade-off between the funnel-facing win and the marketplace-quality cost is more defensible than declaring either side the full story. Option A isolates IKEA's metrics and calls the result an unqualified win, but a routing change that's measurably lowering job quality and pushing away the marketplace's best-rated supply is trading against assets, customer trust and Tasker quality, that the partnership itself ultimately depends on. Option B swings to a full reversion based on ratings alone, discarding IKEA's real, measurable gains without first checking whether a blended routing rule, weighing both speed and rating, could address the quality concern while keeping most of the speed win. Option D reframes success around booking volume, a metric not shown to be at risk in the scenario, and sidesteps the actual, already-visible tension between checkout speed and marketplace quality instead of confronting it.
hints: Three different populations are experiencing three different things here. Ask whether they might be connected through the same routing mechanism rather than being separate stories.
IKEA's win and the marketplace's quality concern may not be independent — check whether the same choice, prioritizing speed over rating, plausibly explains both.

title: IKEA is now the largest revenue partner — leadership wants the routing made permanent
scenario_context: Leadership informs the team that IKEA has just become TaskRabbit's single largest revenue source this quarter, and given that, wants the fastest-arrival IKEA routing rule made permanent policy immediately, without further testing of a blended approach, prioritizing the newly-dominant revenue relationship over the marketplace-quality concerns raised earlier.
description: What's the most defensible response to this instruction?
options: Comply immediately and make fastest-arrival routing permanent, since a company should defer to its largest revenue relationship's priorities without exception.
Refuse the instruction outright, since marketplace quality should never be subordinated to a single commercial partner's metrics regardless of revenue share.
Implement the change, but present leadership with the ratings and retention data alongside the revenue context, and the risk to the IKEA relationship itself.
Delay the decision entirely and commission a six-month study before making any change to the routing rule, given how consequential the revenue relationship now is.
explanation: Option C is correct: leadership's priority shift is a legitimate business input, IKEA's revenue importance is real and worth weighing, but the marketplace-quality risk identified earlier doesn't disappear just because a priority was reassigned, and a team's job here is making sure that risk is visible in the same conversation as the revenue rationale, not silently dropped because a decision was made above them. Surfacing that a declining pool of top-rated Taskers could eventually undermine the exact IKEA relationship being prioritized keeps the full trade-off in front of the actual decision-maker, rather than either blocking the decision or executing it blind to a risk the team already knows about. Option A complies without surfacing information leadership needs to make this call responsibly, treating deference as sufficient when the team holds specific, relevant data leadership may not have fully weighed. Option B refuses outright, but leadership does have the authority to set this priority, and outright refusal isn't a defensible move when the more useful contribution is making sure the decision-maker has the complete picture, not overriding their call unilaterally. Option D stalls a now-time-sensitive business decision with a lengthy study, when a faster path, surfacing the existing data alongside the new priority, gives leadership what they need without an unnecessary and costly delay.
hints: Leadership has the authority to make this call, but that doesn't mean the earlier quality concern should just disappear from the conversation. Ask what the team's actual job is here.
A response that neither blocks the decision nor executes it blindly is available. What would that look like?

title: Now roll fastest-arrival routing out to 20 retail partners at once
scenario_context: TaskRabbit is now considering rolling the fastest-arrival routing model out to 20 different retail partnerships simultaneously, not just IKEA, spanning categories from furniture to appliance installation to TV mounting, each with different typical job complexity and different customer expectations.
description: What's the most defensible way to approach this expansion?
options: Check whether the quality-versus-speed trade-off from IKEA holds across partner categories — a complex install may be far more sensitive to a rushed Tasker than a simple task.
Apply the same fastest-arrival routing rule uniformly across all 20 partners, since the IKEA result already validated the approach and consistency simplifies operations.
Apply fastest-arrival routing only to the 5 largest partners by revenue, and leave the remaining 15 on rating-based routing, using partner size alone as the deciding factor.
Delay the multi-partner rollout entirely until the IKEA routing question itself is fully resolved, since expanding before that decision is finalized would compound an unresolved risk.
explanation: Option A is correct: the IKEA finding was specific to one category of job, furniture assembly, and scaling to 20 categorically different partner types means the same trade-off, speed versus quality, could have very different magnitudes depending on how much a task's difficulty amplifies the cost of routing to a less experienced or lower-rated Tasker. A single uniform rule assumes the IKEA trade-off generalizes evenly across job types with very different complexity and error tolerance, which is exactly the assumption that needs checking before scaling a routing model 20x, rather than after. Option B extrapolates one category's result to nineteen others with different job characteristics, on the assumption that validation in one context transfers cleanly to every other, which is the exact leap a scale-up decision shouldn't make without checking. Option C uses partner revenue size as the sole basis for which routing rule applies, a factor that has no stated connection to which categories are actually more sensitive to the speed-versus-quality trade-off, a smaller partner in a complex, error-prone category could be more at risk than a larger one in a simple category. Option D stalls the entire expansion on resolving a single-partner decision, when the more useful move is actually running the category-sensitivity check this option describes, which can proceed in parallel with, and inform, the IKEA-specific decision rather than blocking on it.
hints: The original trade-off was observed in one specific job category. Ask whether the same trade-off would look identical in a categorically different, more complex kind of task.
Scaling a rule to many new contexts at once is different from scaling the same context to more volume. What would you want to check before assuming one category's result transfers to nineteen others?

title: G2's Satisfaction Score — designing against a fake-account review campaign
scenario_context: G2 ranks B2B software vendors on category pages partly by a 'Satisfaction Score' built from review star ratings. A vendor's competitor discovers that G2 lets any verified user submit a review, and starts a coordinated campaign where its own sales team creates numerous fake small-business accounts to submit glowing reviews of their own product and middling reviews of the rival vendor's product, timed right before the quarterly category-page refresh.
description: Which candidate change to G2's review system would make the Satisfaction Score most resistant to this kind of coordinated fake-account campaign?
options: Require reviews to disclose the reviewer's job title and company name, displayed publicly on the review, to discourage obviously fake submissions.
Increase the minimum review length requirement to 150 words, reasoning that fake reviews are typically short and low-effort.
Allow vendors to publicly flag and dispute any review they believe is fake, removing disputed reviews from the score pending investigation.
Weight reviews by an account-trust signal, verified email domain and account age, so a freshly-created account contributes little at first.
explanation: Option D is correct: the campaign's core capability is creating accounts on demand, so the fix that actually resists it is making a fresh account's influence depend on independently-verifiable signals that accumulate over time and can't be manufactured at the moment of review submission, a domain-verified email, account age, and unrelated prior activity are all things a same-day fake account can't fake into existing history. This forces the attacker to either wait out a long accumulation period, defeating the point of a timed campaign, or accept that their freshly-made accounts barely move the score at all. Option A's disclosure requirement is easily satisfied by a sales team fabricating job titles and company names for accounts they already control, disclosure without independent verification doesn't cost the attacker anything real. Option B's length minimum can be cleared by a coordinated team simply writing longer scripted reviews, a sales team running an organized campaign has every incentive and capability to hit a word count, length alone doesn't require any of the independent history the account-trust approach demands. Option C's dispute mechanism only works after fake reviews are already live and influencing the score during the dispute window, and it puts the burden on vendors to catch and flag each fake review individually rather than making the scoring system itself resistant to the campaign in the first place.
hints: Ask what a coordinated fake-account campaign can create on demand versus what it structurally can't fake in the moment, an account's own history.
